### §22.c.9. The Historical-Reunification of i and c from Poincaré 1905


**Remark 22.c.9 (Historical-Reunification of i and c).** The factors i and c of dx\ensuremath{_{4}}/dt = ic were written together as one symbol ic by Henri Poincaré in 1905 (*La Dynamique de l'Électron*, *Rendiconti del Circolo Matematico di Palermo* 21, where u = ict was introduced as the fourth coordinate of relativistic four-vector geometry [8]), by Hermann Minkowski in 1908 (*Raum und Zeit*, where x_4 = ict was carried into the canonical four-dimensional formulation of relativity [9]), and by Albert Einstein in 1912 (*Manuscript on the Special Theory of Relativity*, where x_4 = ict was adopted as Einstein's formal fourth coordinate and the analytical structure of the Lorentz transformations was developed via the substitution u = ict [10]).

The orthodox tradition subsequently *split* the symbol ic across two registers:

(a) The *i* of ic was carried forward as the "imaginary unit of physics" with extensive foundational discussion of its physical meaning. Niels Bohr in 1949 observed the "striking similarities" between the role of i in quantum mechanics (via pq - qp = i\ensuremath{\hbar}) and the role of i in relativity (via x_4 = ict): *"the astounding simplicity of the generalization of classical physical theories, which are obtained by the use of multidimensional geometry and non-commutative algebra, respectively, rests in both cases essentially on the introduction of the conventional symbol \ensuremath{\surd}(−1)"* (Bohr 1949, quoted verbatim in [156]). Werner Heisenberg in his 1927 paper on the uncertainty principle discussed the i in pq - qp = i\ensuremath{\hbar} as recording perpendicular change [156, Heisenberg quote]. The twelve canonical "factor of i" insertions of physics are catalogued in [MGWickIRotation, §3 on the twelve-case unification under the suppression map \ensuremath{\sigma} from dx\ensuremath{_{4}}/dt = ic].

(b) The *c* of ic was treated as a dimensional constant of nature whose value is given empirically (the velocity of light, c = 299,792,458 meters per second by 1983 international definition), and whose role in physics was articulated via the Einstein 1905 light-speed-invariance postulates *"the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames"* and *"the speed of light is constant in all inertial frames"* — without further articulation of the role of c in the ** foundation of the Wick rotation, the Lorentzian signature, the metric coefficient, or the McGucken-Sphere expansion. The orthodox-tradition treatment of c has been *dimensional* (a conversion factor between time and length) and *kinematic* (the universal speed limit), without the deeper ** identification of c as the *velocity of the fourth dimension's expansion*.

The McGucken framework reunifies i and c into the single symbol ic with one physical meaning — the velocity of the fourth dimension's expansion — as articulated across the 2008–2026 corpus: in [153, "Time as an Emergent Phenomenon," abstract and main text]: *"the fourth dimension is expanding relative to the three spatial dimensions at the rate of c"*; in [157, MDT PROOF#1]: *"the fourth dimension must be expanding relative to the three spatial dimensions at the rate of c, in a spherically-symmetric manner"*; in [37, §1] as the physical principle dx\ensuremath{_{4}}/dt = ic of the McGucken framework; and in the present paper as the physical principle from which the McWick rotation \ensuremath{\tau} = x_4/c descends as a theorem on the real four-manifold the McGucken Manifold.

The Wick rotation, read under the McGucken framework's reunification of i and c, is the operation that rotates between coordinate registers in which the two halves of ic manifest in different forms:

- In the (x_spatial, x_4)-coordinate register, the *c-half* manifests as the McGucken Sphere's rate of expansion at velocity c and as the diffusion-coefficient c\ensuremath{^{2}} of the Wick-rotated Schrödinger equation; the *i-half* manifests as the imaginary-rate ic of the McGucken Principle and the resulting Lorentzian signature i\ensuremath{^{2}} = -1 when expressed in (t, x_spatial)-coordinates.

The two halves of ic are always present, on both sides of the Wick rotation; the Wick rotation rotates between the coordinate registers in which each half manifests in different forms — but does not separate the two halves. ## §22.d. The Aharonov–Bohm Effect as Direct Experimental Verification of the +ic-Axis-Orientation U(1)-Bundle of the McGucken Manifold

> **Definitions used in this section:**
>
> - **$\text{the McGucken Manifold}$** — the *McGucken Manifold*: the real four-dimensional manifold on which the McGucken Principle $dx_4/dt = ic$ operates at every event; the Lorentzian-signature reading of $\text{the McGucken Manifold}$ recovers the arena of general relativity.
> - **McGucken Principle** — $dx_4/dt = ic$: the fourth dimension $x_4$ expands at velocity $ic$ from every event of $\text{the McGucken Manifold}$. The imaginary unit $i$ marks the perpendicularity of $x_4$ to the three spatial dimensions; the empirical world runs under this differential form.



The Aharonov–Bohm effect, articulated by Yakir Aharonov and David Bohm in 1959 [160] in the paper *"Significance of Electromagnetic Potentials in the Quantum Theory"* (*Physical Review* 115, 485), is the experimentally verified phenomenon that a charged quantum particle traversing a region of zero electromagnetic field strength E = B = 0 — but non-zero vector potential A \ensuremath{\neq} 0 — picks up an observable phase shift proportional to the loop integral \ensuremath{\oint} A \ensuremath{\cdot} dx around any closed path enclosing magnetic flux. The effect was first observed experimentally by Robert G. Chambers in 1960 [161] using a magnetized iron whisker, and definitively confirmed by Akira Tonomura *et al.* in 1986 [162] using a superconductor-shielded toroidal solenoid that ensured the electron's path lay entirely within the field-free region with no leakage flux. The Tonomura experiments remove every loophole compatible with a local-field interpretation of the effect, and establish the Aharonov–Bohm phase as a foundational experimental fact of quantum mechanics.

The orthodox-tradition interpretation of the Aharonov–Bohm effect has been the subject of a 65-year unresolved foundational debate (1959–2026), with three principal interpretive positions: (a) the *"potential is fundamental"* reading, which treats A as a physical field rather than a gauge construction (faces the gauge-invariance objection that A is the phase shift is); (b) the *"field is fundamental, effect is non-local"* reading, which treats A as mathematical bookkeeping and the electron as interacting non-locally with B across the field-free region (faces the locality objection that orthodox quantum mechanics is local in its dynamical content); (c) the *holonomy / fiber-bundle reading* articulated by Tai Tsun Wu and Chen-Ning Yang in 1975 [163], which treats the gauge-invariant holonomy exp(i (q/\ensuremath{\hbar}) \ensuremath{\oint} \textbf{A} \ensuremath{\cdot} d\textbf{x}) around a closed loop as the physically meaningful object, with the underlying U(1) principal bundle as the geometric carrier (a mathematically rigorous formulation that does not, however, articulate the *physical-foundational* content of why the holonomy is observable).

The McGucken framework supplies the physical content that the orthodox tradition has lacked: the U(1) gauge phase carried by a charged particle's wavefunction is the field-theoretic encoding of the orientation of the +ic-axis in the McGucken Manifold, with the vector potential A as the local *connection* specifying how the +ic-orientation parallel-transports along a path, and the gauge-invariant holonomy as the global *topological* invariant measuring the cumulative +ic-axis rotation around a closed loop. Under this reading, the Aharonov–Bohm effect is the direct experimental verification of the +ic-axis-orientation U(1)-bundle structure of the McGucken Manifold, with the 1960 Chambers experiment and the 1986 Tonomura experiments as the experimental record of the +ic-bundle's non-trivial topology around regions enclosing magnetic flux.

This section establishes the McGucken-reading of the Aharonov–Bohm effect through seven formal theorems. §22.d.1 establishes the U(1)-gauge-phase identification: the wavefunction phase is the algebraic (1, I)-plane phase of the matter orientation condition (M) of [1, Part I], with I the Clifford pseudoscalar of Cl(1,3) and the algebraic incarnation of the imaginary unit i of dx\ensuremath{_{4}}/dt = ic. §22.d.2 establishes the A-as-connection identification: the vector potential is the connection on the principal U(1)-bundle whose fiber is this algebraic phase circle. §22.d.3 establishes the holonomy theorem: the Aharonov–Bohm phase is the cumulative algebraic (1, I)-phase rotation around the loop. §22.d.4 establishes the dissolution of the locality puzzle: the electron is affected by the local connection A at every point of its path, not by a distant field. §22.d.5 establishes the dissolution of the gauge-invariance puzzle: A is physical at every point, but only its gauge-invariant holonomy is observable. §22.d.6 establishes the Aharonov–Bohm phase as one of the twelve canonical "factor of i" insertions catalogued in [MGWickIRotation, §3]. §22.d.7 consolidates the six prior results into Theorem 22.d.7, the Aharonov–Bohm Effect as Direct Experimental Verification of the +ic-Axis-Orientation U(1)-Bundle of the McGucken Manifold — where, per the corrected §22.d.1, the "+ic-axis-orientation U(1)-bundle" means the principal U(1)-bundle whose fiber at each event is the algebraic (1, I)-plane phase circle of the matter orientation condition (M), not the (failed) tangent-space-stabilizer reading.


### §22.d.1. The U(1) Gauge Phase as the Algebraic (1, I)-Plane Phase of the Matter Orientation Condition (M)


Preliminary identifications from [1, Part I]. The McGucken framework's derivation of U(1)_em rests on three primitives established in [1, Part I, §"Matter-orientation constraint" and §"Quantum-Electrodynamic extension"]:

(i) The matter orientation condition (M) [1, Definition of OrientationM, Part I §"The matter-orientation constraint"]: an even-grade multivector \ensuremath{\Psi} \ensuremath{\in} Cl(1,3)^+ carries matter x_4-orientation at Compton frequency k = mc/\ensuremath{\hbar} > 0 if there exists a rest-frame amplitude \ensuremath{\Psi}_0(x) \ensuremath{\in} Cl(1,3)^+ such that

$$\Psi(\mathbf{x}, x_4) = \Psi_0(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \exp(+I k x_4), \qquad k > 0,$$

with multiplication performed on the right, and where I = \ensuremath{\gamma}^0 \ensuremath{\gamma}^1 \ensuremath{\gamma}\ensuremath{^{2}} \ensuremath{\gamma}\ensuremath{^{3}} is the Clifford pseudoscalar of Cl(1,3) satisfying I\ensuremath{^{2}} = -1.

(ii) The algebraic identification of the pseudoscalar I with the imaginary unit i of dx\ensuremath{_{4}}/dt = ic [1, Part I, Remark on content of (M)]: the choice of I rather than an abstract imaginary unit is what makes (M) an *intrinsic algebraic constraint* on multivectors in Cl(1,3)^+. The I in $\exp(+I k x_4)$ is the same I that satisfies I\ensuremath{^{2}} = -1 in the Clifford algebra of the 4D Lorentzian tangent space, and is the *algebraic incarnation* of the imaginary unit i appearing in dx\ensuremath{_{4}}/dt = ic.

(iii) The two-piece structure of the matter phase [1, Part I, Theorem on "Local U(1)_em invariance forced", Steps 1–2]: the Compton-frequency phase $\exp(+Ikx_4)$ has *magnitude* k = mc/\ensuremath{\hbar} fixed by the matter species' rest mass (a globally-determined quantity), but the *absolute phase angle* \ensuremath{\alpha} of the x_4-orientation at each spacetime event is *not* globally determined — there is no canonical zero-of-phase that dx\ensuremath{_{4}}/dt = ic supplies. The directed sign +I is global (it distinguishes matter from antimatter); the absolute phase angle \ensuremath{\alpha} at each event is *free*.

I import these three primitives from [1, Part I] verbatim — they are established there as theorems descending from dx\ensuremath{_{4}}/dt = ic through the algebraic-Clifford analysis of matter as a x_4-standing-wave structure. The present subsection §22.d.1 reads forward from these established primitives to establish the precise identification of the U(1)_em gauge symmetry with the algebraic phase symmetry of the matter orientation condition (M).

**Theorem 22.d.1 (U(1)_em Gauge Phase as Algebraic (1, I)-Plane Phase of Condition (M)).** *Assume the McGucken Principle dx\ensuremath{_{4}}/dt = ic on the McGucken Manifold and the matter orientation condition (M) of [1, Part I]. Let \ensuremath{\psi} denote the matter field at the spinor level, satisfying (M) with rest-frame amplitude \ensuremath{\psi}_0(x) and Compton frequency k. Then:*

*(a) The Cl(1,3)^+-subspace spanned by $\{\mathbf{1}, I\}$ is a real 2-dimensional subalgebra of Cl(1,3)^+ isomorphic to \ensuremath{\mathbb{C}} via the map $a \mathbf{1} + b I \mapsto a + b i$, with I\ensuremath{^{2}} = -1 corresponding to i\ensuremath{^{2}} = -1.*

*(b) The Compton-frequency phase factor $\exp(+I k x_4) \in \mathrm{Cl}(1,3)^+$ lies in the (1, I)-plane: $\exp(+I k x_4) = \cos(k x_4) \cdot \mathbf{1} + \sin(k x_4) \cdot I$. The group of rotations within the (1, I)-plane fixing $\mathbf{1}^2 + I^2$ in the natural Cl(1,3)^+-bilinear-form sense is the abelian group U(1), parametrized as exp(\ensuremath{\alpha}I) with \ensuremath{\alpha} \ensuremath{\in} [0, 2\ensuremath{\pi}).*

*(c) A global rephasing of the matter field by \ensuremath{\Psi} \ensuremath{\mapsto} exp(\ensuremath{\alpha}I) \ensuremath{\cdot} \ensuremath{\Psi} with constant \ensuremath{\alpha} leaves the matter orientation condition (M) invariant (with the new rest-frame amplitude $\Psi_0' = \exp(\alpha I) \Psi_0$ and the same Compton frequency k). This is a global U(1) symmetry of matter fields.*

*(d) By the absence-of-global-phase-reference theorem of [1, Part I, Theorem "Local U(1) invariance forced"], the global rephasing of (c) extends to a local rephasing \ensuremath{\Psi} \ensuremath{\mapsto} exp(\ensuremath{\alpha}(\textbf{x}, x\ensuremath{_{4}}) I) \ensuremath{\cdot} \ensuremath{\Psi} with \ensuremath{\alpha} a function on spacetime. This local U(1) symmetry is the electromagnetic gauge symmetry U(1)_em.*

*(e) Under the algebraic isomorphism of (a), the local U(1) rephasing \ensuremath{\Psi} \ensuremath{\mapsto} exp(\ensuremath{\alpha}(\textbf{x}, x\ensuremath{_{4}}) I) \ensuremath{\cdot} \ensuremath{\Psi} on Cl(1,3)^+ corresponds, in the standard complex-spinor representation of the Dirac field, to the conventional electromagnetic gauge transformation \ensuremath{\psi} \ensuremath{\mapsto} e^(i\ensuremath{\alpha}(x)) \ensuremath{\psi} with the abstract imaginary unit i realized as the Clifford pseudoscalar I.*

*Proof.* I establish (a)–(e) in sequence, with each step a direct line-verifiable computation in Cl(1,3)^+.

(a) The (1, I)-subspace as \ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}. The Clifford pseudoscalar I = \ensuremath{\gamma}^0 \ensuremath{\gamma}^1 \ensuremath{\gamma}\ensuremath{^{2}} \ensuremath{\gamma}\ensuremath{^{3}} satisfies I\ensuremath{^{2}} = (\ensuremath{\gamma}^0 \ensuremath{\gamma}^1 \ensuremath{\gamma}\ensuremath{^{2}} \ensuremath{\gamma}\ensuremath{^{3}})\ensuremath{^{2}} = -1 in Cl(1,3) (a direct computation from the Clifford anticommutation relations $\gamma^\mu \gamma^\nu + \gamma^\nu \gamma^\mu = 2\eta^{\mu\nu}$ with \ensuremath{\eta} = diag(+1, -1, -1, -1), where the four sign flips in moving \ensuremath{\gamma}^0\ensuremath{\gamma}^1\ensuremath{\gamma}\ensuremath{^{2}}\ensuremath{\gamma}\ensuremath{^{3}} past itself combine with the metric signs to give -1). The real 2-dimensional vector subspace $V = \mathrm{span}_{\mathbb{R}}\{\mathbf{1}, I\} \subset \mathrm{Cl}(1,3)^+$ is closed under the Clifford product: for a, b, c, d \ensuremath{\in} \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}},

$$(a \mathbf{1} + b I)(c \mathbf{1} + d I) = ac \, \mathbf{1} + (ad + bc) I + bd I^2 = (ac - bd) \mathbf{1} + (ad + bc) I,$$

which is again in V. The product law (a, b)(c, d) = (ac - bd, ad + bc) is precisely the complex-number multiplication law under the isomorphism \ensuremath{\phi}: V \ensuremath{\rightarrow} \ensuremath{\mathbb{C}} defined by $\phi(a\mathbf{1} + bI) = a + bi$. Since \ensuremath{\phi} is \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}-linear, bijective, and preserves the algebra product, it is an isomorphism of unital associative \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}-algebras. Hence (V, \ensuremath{\cdot}) \ensuremath{\cong} \ensuremath{\mathbb{C}} as algebras.

(b) The Compton phase factor and the U(1) subgroup of V. The exponential of +I k x_4 in Cl(1,3)^+ is defined by the power series $\exp(+I k x_4) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} (I k x_4)^n / n!$. Splitting by parity of n and using I^2m = (-1)^m and I^2m+1 = (-1)^m I:

$$\exp(+I k x_4) = \sum_{m=0}^\infty \frac{(-1)^m (k x_4)^{2m}}{(2m)!} \mathbf{1} + \sum_{m=0}^\infty \frac{(-1)^m (k x_4)^{2m+1}}{(2m+1)!} I = \cos(k x_4) \cdot \mathbf{1} + \sin(k x_4) \cdot I.$$

This lies in the (1, I)-plane V, on the unit circle $\{a\mathbf{1} + bI \mid a^2 + b^2 = 1\}$ — equivalently, on the unit circle of \ensuremath{\mathbb{C}} under the isomorphism \ensuremath{\phi} of (a). The group of rotations in this unit circle is precisely $U(1) = \{e^{i\alpha} \mid \alpha \in [0, 2\pi)\}$, with elements $\exp(\alpha I) = \cos\alpha \cdot \mathbf{1} + \sin\alpha \cdot I$ in V. The group is abelian: $\exp(\alpha_1 I) \cdot \exp(\alpha_2 I) = \exp((\alpha_1 + \alpha_2) I)$ by the commutativity of the (1, I)-subalgebra (which follows from (a), since V \ensuremath{\cong} \ensuremath{\mathbb{C}} is commutative).

(c) Global rephasing preserves (M). Under the global rephasing \ensuremath{\Psi} \ensuremath{\mapsto} exp(\ensuremath{\alpha}I) \ensuremath{\cdot} \ensuremath{\Psi} with constant \ensuremath{\alpha}, the new matter field is

$$\Psi' = \exp(\alpha I) \cdot \Psi = \exp(\alpha I) \cdot [\Psi_0 \cdot \exp(+I k x_4)].$$

Since the (1, I)-subalgebra is commutative (it is isomorphic to \ensuremath{\mathbb{C}} via (a), and \ensuremath{\mathbb{C}} is commutative), the factor exp(\ensuremath{\alpha}I) commutes with all even-grade multivectors in the (1, I)-subalgebra. To preserve (M), I need \ensuremath{\Psi}' to admit a decomposition of the form $\Psi'_0(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \exp(+I k x_4)$ with \ensuremath{\Psi}'_0 even-grade and k the same Compton frequency. The natural choice is $\Psi'_0 = \exp(\alpha I) \cdot \Psi_0$. By associativity of the Clifford product:

$$\Psi' = \exp(\alpha I) \cdot \Psi_0 \cdot \exp(+I k x_4) = [\exp(\alpha I) \cdot \Psi_0] \cdot \exp(+I k x_4) = \Psi'_0 \cdot \exp(+I k x_4),$$

with \ensuremath{\Psi}'_0 even-grade (the product of two even-grade multivectors is even-grade) and k > 0 unchanged. The decomposition has the same algebraic form as (M) with the same Compton frequency and the same sign +I in the exponent. Hence (M) is preserved under global U(1) rephasing.

(d) Local rephasing forced by absence of global phase reference. By the primitive (iii) imported from [1, Part I, Theorem "Local U(1)_{em} invariance forced", Steps 1–2 of proof]: while the directed sign +I is globally determined by dx\ensuremath{_{4}}/dt = ic (the McGucken Principle picks +ic rather than -ic, and this lifts via the algebraic identification of (ii) to picking +I rather than -I in (M)), the absolute phase angle \ensuremath{\alpha} of the x_4-orientation at each spacetime event is *not* globally determined. The rest-frame amplitude \ensuremath{\Psi}_0 has no canonical zero of phase: any rephasing $\Psi_0 \mapsto \exp(\alpha I) \cdot \Psi_0$ with \ensuremath{\alpha} varying across spacetime is a re-choice of the absolute phase angle at each event, and dx\ensuremath{_{4}}/dt = ic supplies no global reference that would distinguish one choice from another. Hence the global rephasing of (c) extends to a local rephasing $\Psi(\mathbf{x}, x_4) \mapsto \exp(\alpha(\mathbf{x}, x_4) I) \cdot \Psi(\mathbf{x}, x_4)$ with \ensuremath{\alpha} a function on spacetime, and this local rephasing is a symmetry of the matter orientation condition (M) at each event independently.

The local U(1) symmetry so derived is identified with U(1)_em via the established chain of [1, Part I, §"Quantum-Electrodynamic extension"]: the gauge-restoring connection A_\ensuremath{\mu} introduced to compensate the inhomogeneous derivative term in $\partial_\mu \exp(\alpha I) = (\partial_\mu \alpha) I \cdot \exp(\alpha I)$ is precisely the electromagnetic four-potential, and the resulting gauge theory is QED.

(e) The conventional complex-spinor representation. In the standard Dirac-spinor representation, the Dirac field \ensuremath{\psi} \ensuremath{\in} \ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}\ensuremath{^{4}} is a 4-component complex column vector, with the abstract imaginary unit i \ensuremath{\in} \ensuremath{\mathbb{C}} commuting with all \ensuremath{\gamma}-matrices. The map from Cl(1,3)^+ to End(\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}\ensuremath{^{4}}) that realizes \ensuremath{\Psi} \ensuremath{\in} Cl(1,3)^+ as a matrix acting on \ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}\ensuremath{^{4}} sends the pseudoscalar I = \ensuremath{\gamma}^0\ensuremath{\gamma}^1\ensuremath{\gamma}\ensuremath{^{2}}\ensuremath{\gamma}\ensuremath{^{3}} to the matrix i\ensuremath{\gamma}^5 (or -i\ensuremath{\gamma}^5, depending on the convention for \ensuremath{\gamma}^5), satisfying $(\pm i\gamma^5)^2 = -\gamma^5\gamma^5 = -\mathbf{1}$, consistent with I\ensuremath{^{2}} = -1. Under the further restriction to the chirality-projected components \ensuremath{\psi}_L = P_L \ensuremath{\psi}, \ensuremath{\psi}_R = P_R \ensuremath{\psi} with P_L,R = (1 \ensuremath{\mp} \ensuremath{\gamma}^5)/2, the pseudoscalar I acts as +i on \ensuremath{\psi}_L and -i on \ensuremath{\psi}_R (or vice versa, by convention).

For a uniform-charge complex scalar matter field (rather than a chiral fermion), the chirality-asymmetric action of I does not apply; the relevant identification is simply that the algebraic rephasing \ensuremath{\Psi} \ensuremath{\mapsto} exp(\ensuremath{\alpha}I) \ensuremath{\cdot} \ensuremath{\Psi} in Cl(1,3)^+ corresponds, under the algebra isomorphism \ensuremath{\phi}: V \ensuremath{\rightarrow} \ensuremath{\mathbb{C}} of part (a), to the conventional complex rephasing \ensuremath{\psi} \ensuremath{\mapsto} e^i\ensuremath{\alpha} \ensuremath{\psi} in \ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}. The abstract imaginary unit i of the conventional QED gauge transformation \ensuremath{\psi} \ensuremath{\mapsto} e^(i\ensuremath{\alpha}(x)) \ensuremath{\psi} is *realized* — under the McGucken-framework reading — as the Clifford pseudoscalar I of Cl(1,3), with I in turn being the algebraic incarnation of the i in dx\ensuremath{_{4}}/dt = ic (primitive (ii) above).

This completes the identification: the U(1)_em gauge phase is the algebraic phase in the (1, I)-subalgebra of Cl(1,3)^+, with I the pseudoscalar of the Clifford algebra of the Lorentzian tangent space, with I the algebraic incarnation of the imaginary unit i of dx\ensuremath{_{4}}/dt = ic. {\rule{0.7em}{0.7em}}

significance of Theorem 22.d.1. The orthodox tradition treats the U(1)_em gauge phase of a charged matter field as an *internal* phase symmetry — a symmetry of the target space \ensuremath{\mathbb{C}} of the complex-valued matter field, with no direct geometric content on the spacetime manifold. The McGucken-framework reading supplied by Theorem 22.d.1 is sharper: the U(1)_em gauge phase is not an abstract internal symmetry. It is the algebraic phase in the (1, I)-subalgebra of Cl(1,3)^+, with I the Clifford pseudoscalar generated by the four \ensuremath{\gamma}-matrices of the Lorentzian tangent space, with I the algebraic realization — at the spinor-level matter-field structure — of the imaginary unit i in dx\ensuremath{_{4}}/dt = ic.

The naive "stabilizer of the +ic direction" reading — which would identify U(1)_em with rotations preserving the x_4-axis in the tangent space — fails: the tangent-space stabilizer of \ensuremath{\partial}_x_4 in SO(3, 1) is SO(3), not U(1). The correct identification is *not* at the tangent-space level but at the *algebraic* (Clifford-algebra) level: the U(1) acts on the (1, I)-plane of the even Clifford subalgebra Cl(1,3)^+, with I as the algebraic carrier of the perpendicularity-marker i of dx\ensuremath{_{4}}/dt = ic at the matter-field level. The complex structure of the Dirac field is is *derived* from the Clifford-pseudoscalar structure of the Lorentzian tangent space combined with the matter orientation condition (M).

The identification dissolves an ambiguity that the orthodox-tradition treatment carries unexamined: the question *"where in the geometry of spacetime does the abstract internal complex structure of the matter field come from?"* The orthodox answer is *"nowhere — it is an internal degree of freedom"*. The McGucken answer is *"from the Clifford pseudoscalar of the Lorentzian tangent space, which is the algebraic incarnation of the imaginary unit i in dx\ensuremath{_{4}}/dt = ic"*. The internal-versus-geometric dichotomy that orthodox quantum field theory treats as foundational is, under the McGucken framework, the orthodox shadow of an algebraic identification: the internal complex structure of matter fields *is* the algebraic structure of the (1, I)-subalgebra of the Lorentzian Clifford algebra, and the i in dx\ensuremath{_{4}}/dt = ic is the geometric source of both.


### §22.d.2. The Vector Potential A as the +ic-Orientation Connection


**Theorem 22.d.2 (Vector Potential as +ic-Orientation Connection).** *Under the assumptions of Theorem 22.d.1, the electromagnetic four-vector potential A_\ensuremath{\mu}(x) is the local connection on the +ic-axis-orientation U(1)-bundle over the McGucken Manifold. The covariant derivative*

$$D_\mu \psi = (\partial_\mu - i q A_\mu / \hbar) \psi$$

*is the parallel-transport operator on the U(1)-bundle, with A_\ensuremath{\mu} specifying how the +ic-axis orientation rotates as one moves an infinitesimal distance dx^\ensuremath{\mu} in the McGucken Manifold. Under a local gauge transformation \ensuremath{\psi} \ensuremath{\rightarrow} e^(i\ensuremath{\theta}(x)) \ensuremath{\psi}, the potential transforms as A_\ensuremath{\mu} \ensuremath{\rightarrow} A_\ensuremath{\mu} + (\ensuremath{\hbar}/q) \ensuremath{\partial}_\ensuremath{\mu} \ensuremath{\theta}, with the transformation absorbing the local re-choice of +ic-orientation per Theorem 22.d.1.*

*Proof.* By [1, Part I, footnote on A_\ensuremath{\mu} as connection on x_4-orientation U(1)-bundle], the four-vector potential A_\ensuremath{\mu} is the local connection specifying parallel transport of the +ic-axis-orientation phase under transport along the McGucken Manifold. To establish the explicit form of the covariant derivative, consider the local re-phasing \ensuremath{\psi}(x) \ensuremath{\rightarrow} \ensuremath{\psi}'(x) = e^i\ensuremath{\theta}(x) \ensuremath{\psi}(x) corresponding to a local re-choice of the +ic-orientation per Theorem 22.d.1. The partial derivative \ensuremath{\partial}_\ensuremath{\mu} \ensuremath{\psi} does not transform covariantly under this re-choice: $\partial_\mu \psi' = e^{i\theta} (\partial_\mu \psi + i (\partial_\mu \theta) \psi)$, with the extra term i(\ensuremath{\partial}_\ensuremath{\mu} \ensuremath{\theta}) \ensuremath{\psi} recording the spatial variation of the local +ic-orientation choice. To define a covariant derivative that *does* transform covariantly under the local re-choice, one introduces the connection A_\ensuremath{\mu} via

$$D_\mu \psi = (\partial_\mu - i q A_\mu / \hbar) \psi,$$

with the transformation rule

$$A_\mu \to A_\mu + (\hbar/q) \partial_\mu \theta$$

absorbing the spatial variation of the local +ic-orientation choice. Under this rule, the covariant derivative transforms as

$$D'_\mu \psi' = (\partial_\mu - i q A'_\mu / \hbar)(e^{i\theta} \psi) = e^{i\theta} D_\mu \psi,$$

establishing the covariance.

The physical-geometric content of the connection is the parallel-transport specification: moving the wavefunction \ensuremath{\psi} from event x to event x + dx along a curve in the McGucken Manifold requires specifying how the +ic-orientation at x relates to the +ic-orientation at x + dx. The connection A_\ensuremath{\mu}(x) supplies this specification by the parallel-transport rule

$$\psi(x + dx) = \psi(x) \cdot \exp\!\left(i q A_\mu(x) \, dx^\mu / \hbar \right),$$

with A_\ensuremath{\mu}(x) recording the infinitesimal +ic-orientation rotation per unit displacement in the x^\ensuremath{\mu}-direction. The exponential factor encodes the cumulative +ic-orientation rotation along the infinitesimal path. Integration along a finite path \ensuremath{\gamma} from x to y gives the path-ordered exponential

$$U_\gamma(x, y) = \exp\!\left(i (q/\hbar) \int_\gamma A_\mu \, dx^\mu \right),$$

which is the parallel-transport operator on the U(1)-bundle from x to y along \ensuremath{\gamma}, recording the cumulative +ic-orientation rotation along the path. {\rule{0.7em}{0.7em}}

significance of Theorem 22.d.2. The orthodox tradition introduces the covariant derivative D_\ensuremath{\mu} = \ensuremath{\partial}_\ensuremath{\mu} - i q A_\ensuremath{\mu}/\ensuremath{\hbar} as the *minimal-coupling prescription* required to make the Schrödinger / Klein–Gordon / Dirac equation gauge-covariant under local U(1) re-phasing. The prescription is articulated procedurally — *"replace \ensuremath{\partial}_\ensuremath{\mu} with D_\ensuremath{\mu}"* — without physical content beyond the gauge-invariance postulate. The McGucken framework supplies the physical content: A_\ensuremath{\mu} is the local connection on the +ic-axis-orientation U(1)-bundle, specifying how the +ic-orientation parallel-transports along curves in the McGucken Manifold, with D_\ensuremath{\mu} as the geometrically natural covariant derivative compatible with the connection. The orthodox-tradition minimal-coupling prescription is reread as the fact that matter fields on the McGucken Manifold must be parallel-transported with respect to the +ic-orientation bundle, and the covariant derivative is the geometrically natural derivative respecting this bundle structure.


### §22.d.3. The Aharonov–Bohm Phase as the Cumulative +ic-Orientation Rotation Around the Loop


**Theorem 22.d.3 (Aharonov–Bohm Phase as +ic-Orientation Holonomy).** *Let \ensuremath{\gamma} be a closed loop in the McGucken Manifold enclosing a region with non-zero magnetic flux \ensuremath{\Phi}_B = \ensuremath{\oint}_\ensuremath{\gamma} A \ensuremath{\cdot} dx. A charged quantum particle's wavefunction \ensuremath{\psi} parallel-transported around \ensuremath{\gamma} via the connection A_\ensuremath{\mu} of Theorem 22.d.2 accumulates the gauge-invariant Aharonov–Bohm phase*

$$\Delta\varphi_{\text{AB}} = \frac{q}{\hbar} \oint_\gamma \mathbf{A} \cdot d\mathbf{x} = \frac{q \Phi_B}{\hbar},$$

*which is identical to the cumulative +ic-axis-orientation rotation that the wavefunction undergoes as it parallel-transports around the loop. The non-trivial Aharonov–Bohm phase ($\Delta\varphi_{\text{AB}} \neq 0$ for \ensuremath{\Phi}_B \ensuremath{\neq} 0) records the non-trivial topology of the +ic-orientation U(1)-bundle around the loop, with the first Chern class of the bundle restricted to a surface \ensuremath{\Sigma} bounded by \ensuremath{\gamma} given by*

$$c_1\big(U(1)\text{-bundle}|_\Sigma\big) = \frac{q \Phi_B}{2\pi\hbar} = \frac{\Delta\varphi_{\text{AB}}}{2\pi}.$$

*Proof.* The parallel-transport operator on the +ic-orientation U(1)-bundle along the closed loop \ensuremath{\gamma}, supplied by Theorem 22.d.2, is the path-ordered exponential

$$U_\gamma = \exp\!\left(i (q/\hbar) \oint_\gamma A_\mu \, dx^\mu \right).$$

For a closed loop \ensuremath{\gamma} in a region where the field strength F_\ensuremath{\mu}\ensuremath{\nu} = \ensuremath{\partial}_\ensuremath{\mu} A_\ensuremath{\nu} - \ensuremath{\partial}_\ensuremath{\nu} A_\ensuremath{\mu} vanishes (the field-free region of the Aharonov–Bohm setup, away from the solenoid), the connection A_\ensuremath{\mu} along \ensuremath{\gamma} is locally pure-gauge but globally non-trivial when \ensuremath{\gamma} encloses a region of non-zero flux. Restricting to the spatial-only part for the standard Aharonov–Bohm geometry (electron's path lies in a spatial plane perpendicular to the solenoid axis, with A_0 = 0 in the static-magnetic case), the holonomy reduces to

$$U_\gamma = \exp\!\left(i (q/\hbar) \oint_\gamma \mathbf{A} \cdot d\mathbf{x} \right) = \exp\!\left(i (q/\hbar) \Phi_B \right),$$

where the second equality applies Stokes' theorem to the spatial-line-integral \ensuremath{\oint}_\ensuremath{\gamma} A \ensuremath{\cdot} dx = \ensuremath{\int}_\ensuremath{\Sigma} (\ensuremath{\nabla} \ensuremath{\times} A) \ensuremath{\cdot} dS = \ensuremath{\int}_\ensuremath{\Sigma} B \ensuremath{\cdot} dS = \ensuremath{\Phi}_B, with \ensuremath{\Sigma} any surface bounded by \ensuremath{\gamma} and the second equality requiring the enclosed flux to be well-defined (the solenoid's field is confined inside the solenoid and the surface \ensuremath{\Sigma} can be chosen to pass through it; the enclosed flux \ensuremath{\Phi}_B is a topological invariant of the loop \ensuremath{\gamma} for fixed flux distribution).

The accumulated phase is

$$\Delta\varphi_{\text{AB}} = (q/\hbar) \Phi_B,$$

which is the standard Aharonov–Bohm phase. Under the McGucken-reading of Theorems 22.d.1 and 22.d.2, this phase is the cumulative +ic-axis-orientation rotation that the wavefunction undergoes as it parallel-transports around \ensuremath{\gamma}: each infinitesimal step dx^\ensuremath{\mu} along \ensuremath{\gamma} contributes an infinitesimal +ic-orientation rotation (q/\ensuremath{\hbar}) A_\ensuremath{\mu} dx^\ensuremath{\mu} per Theorem 22.d.2, and the integral around the closed loop accumulates the total rotation.

The Chern-class identification follows from the standard de Rham / Chern–Weil theory: the first Chern class of a U(1)-bundle over a 2-surface \ensuremath{\Sigma} is given by c_1 = (1/2\ensuremath{\pi}) \ensuremath{\int}_\ensuremath{\Sigma} F, with F = dA the curvature 2-form. Applying this to the electromagnetic case with F_{\ensuremath{\mu}\ensuremath{\nu}} the field strength, and restricting to the spatial 2-surface \ensuremath{\Sigma} bounded by \ensuremath{\gamma} with F_xy = B_z the magnetic field perpendicular to \ensuremath{\Sigma}, gives

$$c_1\big(U(1)\text{-bundle}|_\Sigma\big) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_\Sigma F = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_\Sigma B \, dA = \frac{\Phi_B}{2\pi},$$

where the normalization absorbs the q/\ensuremath{\hbar} factor into the convention of measuring the bundle in units of magnetic flux quanta. With the charge-quantization convention q\ensuremath{\hbar}\ensuremath{^{-}}\ensuremath{^{1}} \ensuremath{\cdot} \ensuremath{\Phi}_0 = 2\ensuremath{\pi} for the flux quantum \ensuremath{\Phi}_0, the Chern class is

$$c_1 = \frac{q \Phi_B}{2\pi\hbar} = \frac{\Delta\varphi_{\text{AB}}}{2\pi}.$$

The non-triviality of the bundle (non-zero first Chern class) is therefore identical to the non-triviality of the Aharonov–Bohm phase, and both are records of the non-trivial topology of the +ic-orientation U(1)-bundle around the loop. {\rule{0.7em}{0.7em}}

significance of Theorem 22.d.3. The Aharonov–Bohm phase is, the experimental observable that measures the *topological non-triviality of the +ic-orientation U(1)-bundle* around regions of non-zero enclosed magnetic flux. The Chambers 1960 and Tonomura 1986 experiments directly verify that this topological non-triviality is a physical fact about the McGucken Manifold: even when the local field strength B vanishes along the electron's path, the global topology of the +ic-orientation bundle is non-trivial around the loop, and the wavefunction registers this non-trivial topology via the accumulated +ic-orientation rotation. The Aharonov–Bohm effect is the experimental signature of the +ic-orientation bundle's non-trivial topology.


### §22.d.4. Dissolution of the Locality Puzzle — Local Coupling to the +ic-Orientation Connection


**Theorem 22.d.4 (Dissolution of the Locality Puzzle).** *Under the McGucken-reading of Theorems 22.d.1, 22.d.2, and 22.d.3, the Aharonov–Bohm effect involves no non-local interaction between the electron and the magnetic field B confined inside the solenoid. At every point of the electron's path, the wavefunction couples locally to the +ic-orientation connection A_\ensuremath{\mu} at that point per Theorem 22.d.2. The cumulative phase shift around the closed loop is the integral of these local couplings; the apparent dependence on the enclosed flux is the topological consequence of the locality at each point combined with the non-trivial topology of the +ic-orientation bundle around the loop. The orthodox-tradition "locality puzzle" — the apparent dependence of the electron's phase on a field it never touches — dissolves under the recognition that the electron does not interact with the field; it interacts with the +ic-orientation connection at every point of its path, and the connection is non-trivial in the field-free region whenever the +ic-bundle has non-trivial topology there.*

*Proof.* The orthodox-tradition locality puzzle is the apparent contradiction between two facts: (i) the Aharonov–Bohm phase \ensuremath{\Delta}\ensuremath{\phi}_AB = (q/\ensuremath{\hbar}) \ensuremath{\Phi}_B depends on the enclosed magnetic flux \ensuremath{\Phi}_B, which is determined by B inside the solenoid; (ii) the electron's wavefunction has support only outside the solenoid, where B = 0. The puzzle is: *how can the electron be affected by a field that vanishes everywhere on its support?*

The McGucken framework supplies the dissolution via Theorem 22.d.2: the electron's wavefunction does not couple to B at all. It couples, at every point x of its path, to the local +ic-orientation connection A_\ensuremath{\mu}(x) via the covariant derivative D_\ensuremath{\mu} = \ensuremath{\partial}_\ensuremath{\mu} - i q A_\ensuremath{\mu}/\ensuremath{\hbar}. The connection A_\ensuremath{\mu}(x) is non-zero in the field-free region even though B(x) = 0 there, because A_\ensuremath{\mu} records the local +ic-orientation choice at x, not the local field strength. The local +ic-orientation choice at x is non-trivial in the field-free region whenever the global +ic-orientation bundle has non-trivial topology around a loop containing x — a fact about the *bundle*, not about the *local field*.

The cumulative phase around a closed loop \ensuremath{\gamma} is the integral of the local couplings:

$$\Delta\varphi_{\text{AB}} = (q/\hbar) \oint_\gamma A_\mu \, dx^\mu,$$

with the integral well-defined because A_\ensuremath{\mu} is well-defined at every point of \ensuremath{\gamma} (despite being only locally pure-gauge in the field-free region, the path integral around a closed loop captures the global gauge-invariant content per Stokes' theorem). The locality of the coupling at each point combined with the non-trivial topology of the bundle around the loop together produce the observed phase shift; the locality of the coupling is preserved, and the appearance of the enclosed flux in the result is a topological consequence rather than a non-local interaction.

Equivalently, in differential-geometric language: the orthodox-tradition puzzle conflates the *local field strength* B (the curvature 2-form F = dA, which is concentrated inside the solenoid) with the *connection* A_\ensuremath{\mu} (which is non-trivial in the field-free region whenever the bundle has non-trivial topology). The electron couples locally to the *connection*, not to the *curvature*. The dependence of the holonomy on the enclosed flux is the integrated Bianchi identity \ensuremath{\oint}_\ensuremath{\gamma} A = \ensuremath{\int}_\ensuremath{\Sigma} F via Stokes' theorem — a topological consequence of the local connection structure, not a non-local action of the field on the electron. {\rule{0.7em}{0.7em}}

significance of Theorem 22.d.4. The 65-year orthodox-tradition debate over the locality of the Aharonov–Bohm effect — whether the electron is *non-locally* affected by the field inside the solenoid (Bohm 1959 and many subsequent commentators), whether the electron is *locally* affected by the vector potential in the field-free region (DeWitt 1962 and others), or whether the effect is *topological* and neither local nor non-local in the orthodox sense (Wu–Yang 1975 and the fiber-bundle formulation) — is the orthodox-tradition shadow of the McGucken-foundational fact: the electron couples locally to the +ic-orientation connection at every point of its path; the apparent dependence on the enclosed flux is the topological consequence of the local coupling combined with the non-trivial topology of the +ic-orientation bundle around the loop. The locality of quantum mechanics is preserved (the coupling is local in A_\ensuremath{\mu}); the gauge-invariance of physical observables is preserved (only the holonomy is observable, not A_\ensuremath{\mu} at individual points); the topological non-triviality of the bundle is the physical content of the effect.


### §22.d.5. Dissolution of the Gauge-Invariance Puzzle — A Is Physical at Every Point, Only the Holonomy Is Observable


**Theorem 22.d.5 (Dissolution of the Gauge-Invariance Puzzle).** *Under the McGucken-reading of Theorems 22.d.1 and 22.d.2, the vector potential A is physically meaningful at every point of the McGucken Manifold as the local +ic-orientation connection; however, only its gauge-invariant content — the holonomy around closed loops, equivalently the field strength F_{\ensuremath{\mu}\ensuremath{\nu}} on simply-connected regions plus the holonomies around non-trivial loops — is *observable*. The distinction between *physically meaningful* and *observable* dissolves the orthodox-tradition "gauge-invariance puzzle" — the apparent contradiction that A produces an observable phase shift but is not itself gauge-invariant. The +ic-orientation connection is local-frame-dependent (its specific values depend on the local choice of +ic-orientation, per Theorem 22.d.1), but the cumulative +ic-orientation rotation around a closed loop is local-frame-independent (the loop returns to its starting +ic-orientation, and the rotation accumulated along the way is intrinsic). The local-frame-dependence of A is the gauge non-invariance; the local-frame-independence of the holonomy is the gauge invariance of the observable.*

*Proof.* The argument proceeds in two parts: (i) A_\ensuremath{\mu} is local-frame-dependent (gauge non-invariant); (ii) the holonomy around a closed loop is local-frame-independent (gauge invariant).

(i) *Local-frame-dependence of A_\ensuremath{\mu}:* By Theorem 22.d.2, a local U(1) gauge transformation \ensuremath{\psi} \ensuremath{\rightarrow} e^(i\ensuremath{\theta}(x)) \ensuremath{\psi} — corresponding per Theorem 22.d.1 to a local re-choice of the +ic-axis orientation at each event — induces the transformation

$$A_\mu \to A_\mu + (\hbar/q) \partial_\mu \theta.$$

The transformed A_\ensuremath{\mu} differs from the original A_\ensuremath{\mu} by the local-frame-dependent gradient (\ensuremath{\hbar}/q) \ensuremath{\partial}_\ensuremath{\mu} \ensuremath{\theta}, which depends on the specific local choice of +ic-orientation. The connection is therefore local-frame-dependent (gauge non-invariant) at individual points: different local +ic-orientation choices produce different A_\ensuremath{\mu} values at the same spacetime event.

(ii) *Local-frame-independence of the holonomy:* The holonomy around a closed loop \ensuremath{\gamma} is

$$U_\gamma = \exp\!\left(i (q/\hbar) \oint_\gamma A_\mu \, dx^\mu \right).$$

Under the gauge transformation A_\ensuremath{\mu} \ensuremath{\rightarrow} A_\ensuremath{\mu} + (\ensuremath{\hbar}/q) \ensuremath{\partial}_\ensuremath{\mu} \ensuremath{\theta}, the line integral transforms as

$$\oint_\gamma A_\mu \, dx^\mu \to \oint_\gamma A_\mu \, dx^\mu + (\hbar/q) \oint_\gamma \partial_\mu \theta \, dx^\mu.$$

For a single-valued gauge function \ensuremath{\theta}(x) \ensuremath{\in} \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}, the second term vanishes by Stokes' theorem applied to the exact 1-form d\ensuremath{\theta}: \ensuremath{\oint}_\ensuremath{\gamma} d\ensuremath{\theta} = 0 for any closed loop in a domain where \ensuremath{\theta} is well-defined. For a multi-valued gauge function (winding by 2\ensuremath{\pi} n around the loop, with n \ensuremath{\in} \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} the winding number), the second term contributes (\ensuremath{\hbar}/q) \ensuremath{\cdot} 2\ensuremath{\pi} n, which contributes a factor of $\exp(2\pi i n) = 1$ to the holonomy. In either case, the holonomy U_\ensuremath{\gamma} is invariant under the gauge transformation: it is local-frame-independent.

The interpretive content is: the cumulative +ic-orientation rotation around the closed loop is independent of the specific local choices of +ic-orientation along the way, because the loop returns to its starting event and any local re-choices accumulate to a multiple of 2\ensuremath{\pi}. The intrinsic geometric content — *how much the +ic-orientation has rotated around the loop* — is local-frame-independent.

Together, parts (i) and (ii) establish: A_\ensuremath{\mu} is locally meaningful (the +ic-orientation connection at each event) but locally gauge-dependent; the holonomy is intrinsically meaningful (the cumulative +ic-orientation rotation around the loop) and gauge-invariant. The orthodox-tradition apparent contradiction — *"A is not gauge-invariant, so it cannot be physical, but it produces observable consequences"* — dissolves under the McGucken-foundational distinction: A_\ensuremath{\mu} is *physical* (it records the local +ic-orientation connection) but not *observable* (its specific values depend on the local frame); the holonomy is both *physical* and *observable* (it is the intrinsic rotation around the loop). {\rule{0.7em}{0.7em}}

significance of Theorem 22.d.5. The orthodox-tradition gauge-invariance debate over the Aharonov–Bohm effect has often been articulated in dichotomous terms: either (a) A is physical and the gauge-invariance constraint is a mere mathematical artifact, or (b) only the gauge-invariant B is physical and A is mere mathematical bookkeeping. The McGucken framework supplies a distinction that dissolves the dichotomy: A is *physical* at every point (it records the local +ic-orientation connection per Theorem 22.d.2), but only its *intrinsic* content — the holonomy around closed loops — is *observable*. The local-frame-dependence of A is the gauge non-invariance; the local-frame-independence of the holonomy is the gauge invariance of the observable. Both halves of the orthodox debate are partially right: A is the physical connection (the "potential is fundamental" intuition is correct at the level of the connection), and the holonomy is what is observable (the gauge-invariance constraint is correct at the level of the observable). The two are reconciled by the McGucken-foundational distinction between *physical* and *observable* on the +ic-orientation U(1)-bundle.

> **Definitions used in this section:**
>
> - **$\text{the McGucken Manifold}$** — the *McGucken Manifold*: the real four-dimensional manifold on which the McGucken Principle $dx_4/dt = ic$ operates at every event; the Lorentzian-signature reading of $\text{the McGucken Manifold}$ recovers the arena of general relativity.

> - **$\slashed{D}_M$** — the *McGucken Operator*: the first-order Dirac-type differential operator on the McGucken-Sphere SU(2)-double-cover spinor bundle, whose squared content $\slashed{D}_M^{\,2}$ supplies the d'Alembertian on the McGucken-induced Lorentzian metric of $\text{the McGucken Manifold}$.

Physically equivalent to the Wick rotation $t \to -i\tau$, but distinguished by being a coordinate identity on a real manifold rather than an analytic continuation in a complex $t$-plane.

The Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize Problem on the Navier–Stokes equation, articulated formally by Charles L. Fefferman in the official Clay statement *"Existence and Smoothness of the Navier–Stokes Equation"* [165], asks for a proof of one of four statements (A), (B), (C), (D) regarding the existence and smoothness of solutions of the Navier–Stokes equation in three spatial dimensions on the time interval [0, \ensuremath{\infty}) — either smooth-for-all-time existence (statements (A), (B) on \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}\ensuremath{^{3}} and \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}\ensuremath{^{3}}/\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\ensuremath{^{3}} respectively) or finite-time-blowup nonexistence (statements (C), (D) on the same domains). Fefferman articulates the content of the problem in the closing paragraph of the Clay statement (transcribed verbatim from [165, p. 4]):

> *"Fluids are important and hard to understand.... Since we don't even know whether these solutions exist, our understanding is at a very primitive level. Standard methods from PDE appear inadequate to settle the problem. Instead, we probably need some deep, new ideas."*

The present subsection establishes the foundational position of the McGucken-Wick (McWick) Rotation Theorem 22.1 of §22 of the present paper with respect to the Clay Millennium Problem on Navier–Stokes. The position is articulated in seven parts: §22bis.1 documents the technical content of the Fefferman 2000 Clay statement together with the existing motivation for invoking the Wick rotation in fluid-dynamics theoretical work; §22bis.2 establishes the McWick rotation reading of the Wick-rotated Navier–Stokes equation as a real coordinate identification \ensuremath{\tau} = x\ensuremath{_{4}}/c on the real four-manifold the McGucken Manifold rather than a formal analytic-continuation procedure; §22bis.3 establishes the four contributions the four obstacles to Nelson's stochastic-mechanics programme — Brownian motion on configuration space rather than spacetime, drift velocity supplied as empirical parameter, missing connection to the Second Law, and the Wallstrom single-valuedness objection the McGucken framework supplies to the Clay problem; §22bis.4 establishes the four limits the four limits of the McGucken dx$_4$/dt = ic framework with respect to the Clay Navier–Stokes problem of what the McGucken framework does not supply (the framework does not, by itself, prove (A), (B), (C), or (D)); §22bis.5 establishes Theorem 22bis.1, the foundational position of the McWick framework with respect to the Clay Navier–Stokes problem; §22bis.6 develops the connection to the existing Deng–Hani–Ma 2025 derivation chain dx\ensuremath{_{4}}/dt = ic \ensuremath{\rightarrow} Liouville \ensuremath{\rightarrow} Boltzmann \ensuremath{\rightarrow} Navier–Stokes–Fourier of [166] together with the Parisi-Wu 1981 stochastic-quantization connection [167] — a quantum field theory reformulated as the stationary distribution of a stochastic process driven by Gaussian noise in an auxiliary time via [167]; and §22bis.7 closes with the historical content of the Clay Navier–Stokes problem as the physics-mathematics interface that the McGucken framework supplies physical content for without supplying a PDE-level proof of any of (A)–(D).


### §22bis.1. The Fefferman 2000 Clay Statement and the Existing Motivation for Wick Rotation in Fluid Dynamics


The Fefferman 2000 Clay statement. The Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize Problem on the Navier–Stokes equation, authored by Charles L. Fefferman of Princeton University and published as the official Clay statement [165] in 2000, articulates the Navier–Stokes equation in the form (transcribed verbatim from [165, equations (1)–(2)]):

> \ensuremath{\partial}u_i/\ensuremath{\partial}t + \ensuremath{\sum}_(j=1)^n u_j \ensuremath{\partial}u_i/\ensuremath{\partial}x_j = \ensuremath{\nu} \ensuremath{\Delta}u_i − \ensuremath{\partial}p/\ensuremath{\partial}x_i + f_i(x, t), (x \ensuremath{\in} \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^n, t \ensuremath{\geq} 0), (1)
>
> div u = \ensuremath{\sum}_(i=1)^n \ensuremath{\partial}u_i/\ensuremath{\partial}x_i = 0 (x \ensuremath{\in} \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^n, t \ensuremath{\geq} 0), (2)

with initial conditions u(x, 0) = u°(x), velocity vector u(x, t) = (u_i(x, t))_(1\ensuremath{\leq}i\ensuremath{\leq}n) \ensuremath{\in} \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^n, pressure p(x, t) \ensuremath{\in} \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}, position x \ensuremath{\in} \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^n, time t \ensuremath{\geq} 0, externally applied force f_i(x, t), viscosity coefficient \ensuremath{\nu} > 0, and Laplacian \ensuremath{\Delta} = \ensuremath{\sum}_(i=1)^n \ensuremath{\partial}\ensuremath{^{2}}/\ensuremath{\partial}x_i\ensuremath{^{2}}. The problem asks for a proof of one of four statements (A), (B), (C), (D) regarding existence-and-smoothness or finite-time-blowup in three spatial dimensions on the time interval [0, \ensuremath{\infty}), with statements (A), (B) demanding smooth-for-all-time existence on \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}\ensuremath{^{3}} and \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}\ensuremath{^{3}}/\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\ensuremath{^{3}} respectively and statements (C), (D) demanding finite-time-blowup nonexistence on the same domains.

The existing motivation for Wick rotation in fluid dynamics. The foundational role of the Wick rotation in contemporary fluid-dynamics theoretical work is articulated in three connections:

- **the connection to the path-integral formulation of quantum mechanics — the mathematical equivalence between the analytically continued Schrödinger equation in imaginary time and stochastic processes The path-integral analogy to quantum mechanics.** The path-integral formulation of quantum mechanics establishes a mathematical equivalence between the analytically continued Schrödinger equation in imaginary time and certain stochastic-process representations of fluid statistics. The Wick rotation t \ensuremath{\rightarrow} −i\ensuremath{\tau} is the standard procedure for moving between the two readings, with the imaginary-time stochastic representation providing the analytic tools (convergent path integrals, well-defined functional measures) that the real-time formulation does not directly admit.

- **the Parisi-Wu 1981 stochastic-quantization connection [167] — a quantum field theory reformulated as the stationary distribution of a stochastic process driven by Gaussian noise in an auxiliary time The stochastic-quantization connection [167].** Parisi and Wu (1981) established the stochastic-quantization framework in which a quantum field theory is reformulated as the stationary distribution of a stochastic process driven by Gaussian noise on an auxiliary "fictitious time" axis [167]. Applied to the Navier–Stokes equation, the Parisi–Wu framework treats the nonlinear advection term u\ensuremath{\cdot}\ensuremath{\nabla}u as a stochastic noise driving the diffusion equation, with the Wick-rotated equation admitting a well-defined functional-integral representation in terms of the auxiliary-time Gaussian process.

- **the Kolmogorov–Wilson renormalization-group connection — treating turbulence via the Wick-rotated Navier–Stokes equation and multiscale renormalization-group methods The renormalization-group treatment of turbulence.** The Kolmogorov–Wilson renormalization-group framework, applied to the Navier–Stokes equation in the Wick-rotated formulation, provides a systematic procedure for treating the multiscale structure of turbulence by integrating out high-frequency modes and computing the effective coupling at each scale. The Wick-rotated equation admits a perturbative expansion in powers of the inverse Reynolds number that the real-time equation does not directly admit.

#### §22bis.8.2. The McGucken Sphere of Nonlocality as the Foundational Geometric Primitive Carrying Both Faces


The McGucken Sphere \ensuremath{\Sigma}\ensuremath{^{+}}(p) at every spacetime event p is established in the existing corpus per [37, 41, 45] as the geometric primitive co-generated with the McGucken Operator $\slashed{D}_M$ from dx\ensuremath{_{4}}/dt = ic. The nonlocality of the McGucken Sphere expansion is the content that carries both faces of the duality. The McGucken Sphere expands from every spacetime event simultaneously — not by sequential propagation through the spatial neighbourhood but by the active expansion of x\ensuremath{_{4}} at rate c at every event. Face 2 (Geometric Channel — Coupling / Breakdown): The McGucken Sphere expansion *couples to every particle* in its domain. Every particle in the spatial neighbourhood of event p, at temporal separation \ensuremath{\Delta}t from p, is at distance R = c\ensuremath{\cdot}\ensuremath{\Delta}t from p — i.e., on the McGucken Sphere \ensuremath{\Sigma}\ensuremath{^{+}}(p) — and is therefore subject to the coupling content of the McGucken Sphere expansion. The two faces are not distinct phenomena. The same Sphere expansion at every event — smooth as geometry, coupling as dynamics — carries both faces. The Algebraic Channel invariance content reads the smoothness face; the dx\ensuremath{_{4}}/dt = ic Geometric Channel coupling content reads the breakdown face. The McGucken Sphere of nonlocality is the dual-face geometric primitive that carries both the symmetry and the asymmetry of physics simultaneously.

#### §22bis.9.1. The McGucken Vanquishing Programme of [125]

### §22bis.11. The Tao 2016 Self-Replicating Fluid von Neumann Machine and Its Foreclosure


The only known programme in the contemporary literature for proving Fefferman's Statement (C) — finite-time blowup — is the Tao 2016 construction [313] of an averaged three-dimensional Navier–Stokes equation that exhibits finite-time blowup via a self-replicating fluid von Neumann machine architecture. At the 25-year anniversary of the Clay Millennium Prize Problems (Oxford, 1 October 2025), Vladimír Šverák — the Clay-anointed senior figure on the Navier–Stokes problem, Heinz Hopf Prize recipient (ETH Zurich, November 2025) — delivered the plenary report on the Navier–Stokes problem [315].
