### §29.7.1. The Pre-McGucken Spinor — Seven Layers of Phenomenological Necessity Without Foundational Origin


The pre-McGucken spinor is a layered accretion of formal-mathematical content built up over a hundred years, with each historical layer added when an earlier formulation proved insufficient and no single layer being foundational. The present subsection documents the seven canonical historical layers.


Layer 1 (Cartan 1913). A spinor is an element of a vector space carrying an irreducible representation of the Clifford algebra Cl(p,q) over a real quadratic form of signature (p,q). Élie Cartan introduced spinors in his 1913 paper *"Les groupes projectifs qui ne laissent invariante aucune multiplicité plane"* as algebraic objects on which the orthogonal-group Lie algebra acts via the Clifford-algebra representation. The Clifford algebra is generated by elements \ensuremath{\gamma}^\ensuremath{\mu} (\ensuremath{\mu} = 1, …, p+q) satisfying the anticommutator relations


$$\{\gamma^\mu, \gamma^\nu\} = \gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu + \gamma^\nu\gamma^\mu = 2\eta^{\mu\nu}\,\mathbb{1}$$


with $\eta^{\mu\nu}$ the metric of signature (p,q). The spinor space is the irreducible representation of Cl(p,q). *This is the most algebraically primitive pre-McGucken definition: a spinor is whatever the Clifford algebra acts on irreducibly.*


Layer 2 (Pauli 1925–1927). A spinor is a two-component complex object \ensuremath{\psi} = (\ensuremath{\psi}_+, \ensuremath{\psi}_-)^T \ensuremath{\in} \ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}\ensuremath{^{2}} that picks up a sign (-1) under a 2\ensuremath{\pi} rotation in three-dimensional Euclidean space, with full identity restoration requiring a 4\ensuremath{\pi} rotation. The Pauli spinor formulation captured the empirical fact, established experimentally through the Stern-Gerlach experiment (1922) and the Goudsmit-Uhlenbeck hypothesis (1925), that electron spin requires a representation of the rotation group in which a single rotation by 2\ensuremath{\pi} does *not* return the state to itself. Pauli formalized this in his 1927 paper by exhibiting the representation under SU(2), which double-covers SO(3) via the surjective Lie-group homomorphism $\mathrm{SU}(2) \twoheadrightarrow \mathrm{SO}(3)$ with kernel $\{+\mathbb{1}, -\mathbb{1}\} \cong \mathbb{Z}_2$. *This double-cover property is the second pre-McGucken layer: spinors transform under SU(2), which double-covers the rotation group SO(3).*


Layer 3 (Dirac 1928). A spinor is a four-component complex object \ensuremath{\psi} \ensuremath{\in} \ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}\ensuremath{^{4}} that transforms under the Lorentz group SO^+(1,3) via the Dirac representation \ensuremath{\rho}_D: Spin(1,3) \ensuremath{\rightarrow} GL(\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}\ensuremath{^{4}}). Dirac introduced the four-component Dirac spinor in his 1928 paper *"The Quantum Theory of the Electron"* by demanding a relativistic wave equation linear in the time-derivative, leading to the Dirac equation


$$\big(i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu - m\big)\psi = 0$$


with \ensuremath{\gamma}^\ensuremath{\mu} (\ensuremath{\mu} = 0, 1, 2, 3) the Dirac gamma matrices. The four components of the Dirac spinor split into a particle/antiparticle plus spin-up/spin-down structure, with the Dirac equation supplying the relativistic dynamical content. *The third pre-McGucken layer: the Dirac equation is a postulated dynamical equation whose specific structure (linear in \ensuremath{\partial}_t, with \ensuremath{\gamma}^\ensuremath{\mu} matrices, with mass term m) is constrained by Lorentz covariance and the requirement of producing the Klein-Gordon equation upon squaring, but is not derived from any deeper physical principle.*


Layer 4 (Weyl 1929). A spinor decomposes into chiral components \ensuremath{\psi}_L and \ensuremath{\psi}_R transforming under the two SU(2) factors of Spin(1,3) \ensuremath{\cong} SL(2,\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}). Hermann Weyl introduced the chiral spinor decomposition in his 1929 paper *"Elektron und Gravitation"*: the Dirac spinor \ensuremath{\psi} in the Weyl basis takes the form \ensuremath{\psi} = (\ensuremath{\psi}_L, \ensuremath{\psi}_R)^T with \ensuremath{\psi}_L transforming under the left-handed SU(2)_L representation and \ensuremath{\psi}_R transforming under the right-handed SU(2)_R representation. In Euclidean signature, the universal cover Spin(4) \ensuremath{\cong} SU(2)_L \ensuremath{\times} SU(2)_R supplies two independent SU(2) factors — the structure Woit 2026 builds his Euclidean Twistor Unification on. *The fourth pre-McGucken layer: the chirality decomposition is an empirical feature of the Standard Model (parity violation in weak interactions selects the SU(2)_L factor for charged-current couplings), but its foundational origin is not articulated in the orthodox tradition.*


Layer 5 (Cartan 1929 — Brauer-Weyl 1935 — Geroch 1968). A spinor is a section of a spinor bundle over a manifold M. When spinors are defined on a curved manifold rather than flat space, they become sections of a fiber bundle whose fibers are the spinor representation spaces and whose transition functions are spinor-bundle transformations. The existence of a global spinor bundle requires the manifold to be *spin* — a topological condition involving the vanishing of the second Stiefel-Whitney class w_2(M) = 0 — and even when this condition is met, the spinor bundle may be non-trivial and may admit inequivalent spin structures (Geroch 1968). *The fifth pre-McGucken layer: spinor structures require global topological conditions on the manifold whose foundational origin is not articulated.*


Layer 6 (Penrose 1967). A spinor is more fundamental than a vector; vectors are constructed from pairs of spinors as $v^\mu = \bar{\psi}\gamma^\mu\psi$ (bilinear form). Penrose's 1967 twistor program inverts the usual hierarchy: instead of spinors being defined relative to a metric (via the Clifford algebra), the metric and the vector space are constructed from spinors as bilinear constructs. The twistor space \ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}\ensuremath{^{3}} is the natural arena, with spinors \ensuremath{\psi} \ensuremath{\in} \ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}\ensuremath{^{2}} at every point of Minkowski space encoding both position and null direction. *The sixth pre-McGucken layer: the spinor-precedes-vector inversion is suggestive but the foundational origin of the spinor itself remains unarticulated; Penrose's program supplies elegant mathematics but no deeper physical principle.*


Layer 7 (Atiyah-Singer 1971–1984; Connes 1985–1994). A spinor is the canonical local representation of the Dirac operator on a spin manifold, with the Dirac operator D = \ensuremath{\gamma}^\ensuremath{\mu}\ensuremath{\nabla}_\ensuremath{\mu} encoding the manifold's metric and spin structure. The Atiyah-Singer index theorem (1963, with subsequent refinements) and Connes' noncommutative-geometry program (1985–1994) supply the spectral characterization: a spin manifold is recovered from the spectral triple (\ensuremath{\mathcal{A}}, \ensuremath{\mathcal{H}}, D) where \ensuremath{\mathcal{A}} is the algebra of smooth functions, \ensuremath{\mathcal{H}} is the spinor Hilbert space, and D is the Dirac operator. *The seventh pre-McGucken layer: the spinor is the canonical Hilbert-space carrier of the Dirac operator's spectral content, with the spectral triple encoding the manifold's geometry — but the foundational origin of the spinor representation itself is not articulated.*


The pre-McGucken status of the spinor. A spinor is something whose nature is articulated through a *combination* of the seven layers, with no single layer being foundational. Cartan's algebraic definition does not explain *why* the Clifford algebra is the right algebra; the Pauli double-cover does not explain *why* fermions need a double-cover representation; the Dirac equation is *postulated* with its specific form rather than derived; the chirality decomposition is *observed* in the Standard Model without foundational origin; the spinor bundle requires *topological assumptions* on the manifold; the Penrose twistor inversion is an *alternative formulation* without explanation of why it works; the noncommutative-geometry formulation *encodes* the structure without explaining its origin.


Pauli's reported remark that spinors were "more mysterious than the imaginary unit" articulates the foundational status of the pre-McGucken spinor: a phenomenologically necessary object whose foundational origin has remained unresolved across a hundred years of orthodox-tradition mathematical sophistication. Cartan himself called spinors *"imaginary curves in space"* in his 1938 book *"The Theory of Spinors"*, exhibiting the orthodox-tradition recognition that the spinor's nature has not been articulated. The mystery is, not just expository: there is no orthodox-tradition derivation of the spinor's existence from a more foundational principle. The spinor is taken as a postulated primitive whose form is constrained by experimental data (electron spin = ½, electron magnetic moment g \ensuremath{\approx} 2, parity violation in weak interactions) and by mathematical consistency requirements (Lorentz covariance, double-cover representation, Clifford algebra structure).


### §29.7.2. The Foundational Fact — The Asymmetry Between Rotation in the Spatial Slice and Rotation into x\ensuremath{_{4}}


Before establishing the McGucken-framework derivation of the spinor as a theorem of dx\ensuremath{_{4}}/dt = ic, the present subsection identifies the foundational fact that the derivation depends on: the asymmetry between rotation within the spatial slice (x\ensuremath{_{1}}, x\ensuremath{_{2}}, x\ensuremath{_{3}}) and rotation into the fourth dimension x\ensuremath{_{4}}. This asymmetry, which is dynamically encoded in the McGucken Principle dx\ensuremath{_{4}}/dt = ic, is the geometric fact underlying every aspect of the spinor's phenomenology and underlying at least ten empirically-observed phenomena that the orthodox tradition has documented without recognizing the unified foundational origin.


The asymmetry, stated precisely. In the McGucken framework, the four coordinates (x\ensuremath{_{1}}, x\ensuremath{_{2}}, x\ensuremath{_{3}}, x\ensuremath{_{4}}) of the McGucken Manifold are not dynamically equivalent. The three spatial coordinates (x\ensuremath{_{1}}, x\ensuremath{_{2}}, x\ensuremath{_{3}}) are *static*: they label fixed positions in space at a given moment, with no intrinsic dynamics. The fourth coordinate x\ensuremath{_{4}} is *expanding*: it is physically advancing at velocity c from every event via dx\ensuremath{_{4}}/dt = ic, with the imaginary unit \ensuremath{i} encoding the perpendicularity of x\ensuremath{_{4}} to the three spatial dimensions.


The kinematic content of the asymmetry, stated precisely. When an object (a particle, a spin, a vector, a wavefunction) is rotated within the spatial slice — that is, transformed by an element of SO(3) acting on (x\ensuremath{_{1}}, x\ensuremath{_{2}}, x\ensuremath{_{3}}) — the rotation is *closed and static*: the rotation group SO(3) is compact (a closed, bounded Lie group), a rotation by 2\ensuremath{\pi} returns to the identity, and the rotated object does not acquire any new motion. When the same object is rotated *into* x\ensuremath{_{4}} — that is, transformed by a boost or by an embedding into the fourth-dimensional direction — the rotation is *open and dynamic*: the boost group is non-compact (an unbounded Lie group), arbitrary rapidity parameters are allowed without ever returning to identity, and the rotated object acquires the velocity c along the x\ensuremath{_{4}}-direction because x\ensuremath{_{4}} is dynamically expanding at c from every event.


The single sentence that captures the foundational asymmetry: rotation within the spatial slice is closed-and-static (the spatial slice does not move, so the rotation returns to identity at 2\ensuremath{\pi}); rotation into x\ensuremath{_{4}} is open-and-dynamic (the x\ensuremath{_{4}}-axis is expanding at c via dx\ensuremath{_{4}}/dt = ic, so rotation into it picks up the velocity c and never closes back on itself).


**Theorem 29.7.2.1 (Asymmetry as a Direct Consequence of dx\ensuremath{_{4}}/dt = ic).** *The asymmetry between rotation within (x\ensuremath{_{1}}, x\ensuremath{_{2}}, x\ensuremath{_{3}}) and rotation into x\ensuremath{_{4}} is a direct theorem of the McGucken Principle. Specifically:*


*(a) The spatial rotation group acting on (x\ensuremath{_{1}}, x\ensuremath{_{2}}, x\ensuremath{_{3}}) is SO(3), which is compact: a rotation by parameter \ensuremath{\theta} \ensuremath{\in} [0, 2\ensuremath{\pi}) returns to identity at \ensuremath{\theta} = 2\ensuremath{\pi}.*


*(b) The boost group acting on the x\ensuremath{_{4}}-direction is non-compact: a boost by rapidity \ensuremath{\zeta} \ensuremath{\in} \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}} does not return to identity for any finite \ensuremath{\zeta}, and the boosted velocity $v = c\tanh\zeta$ approaches but never reaches c as \ensuremath{\zeta} \ensuremath{\rightarrow} \ensuremath{\infty}.*


*(c) The compact/non-compact distinction between SO(3) (spatial) and the boost group (into-x\ensuremath{_{4}}) is the algebraic-shadow articulation of the McGucken framework's fact that the spatial slice is static while x\ensuremath{_{4}} is dynamically expanding at c.*


**Proof.** Parts (a) and (b) are standard Lie-group facts about SO(3) and the Lorentz boost group. Part (c) is the McGucken-framework identification.


For Part (a): the rotation group SO(3) acts on the unit sphere S\ensuremath{^{2}} in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}\ensuremath{^{3}}, with the action being transitive and the stabilizer of any point being SO(2). The compactness of SO(3) follows from the compactness of S\ensuremath{^{2}} \ensuremath{\cong} SO(3)/SO(2) as a topological space. A rotation by angle \ensuremath{\theta} around any axis returns to identity at \ensuremath{\theta} = 2\ensuremath{\pi}.


For Part (b): the Lorentz boost in direction n̂ with rapidity \ensuremath{\zeta} acts on the time-coordinate and the n̂-spatial-coordinate via $(ct', x'_\parallel) = (\cosh\zeta \cdot ct - \sinh\zeta \cdot x_\parallel, -\sinh\zeta \cdot ct + \cosh\zeta \cdot x_\parallel)$, with x_\ensuremath{\perp} unchanged. The boost generators are K_i = i(x_0\ensuremath{\partial}_i + x_i\ensuremath{\partial}_0), and they satisfy the Lie-algebra relation [K_i, K_j] = -i\ensuremath{\varepsilon}_ijkJ_k where J_k are the rotation generators (the negative sign in the commutator distinguishes boosts from rotations and is the origin of the boost group's non-compactness). The boosted velocity $v = c\tanh\zeta$ satisfies $\lim_{\zeta \to \infty} v = c$, with no finite rapidity returning the boost to identity.


For Part (c): the McGucken framework's fact is that the spatial slice (x\ensuremath{_{1}}, x\ensuremath{_{2}}, x\ensuremath{_{3}}) at any given x\ensuremath{_{4}}-time is a static three-manifold (no intrinsic motion within the slice), while the x\ensuremath{_{4}}-axis is dynamically expanding at velocity c via dx\ensuremath{_{4}}/dt = ic. The compactness of SO(3) is the algebraic-shadow articulation of the staticity of the spatial slice: the slice has no intrinsic dynamics, so rotations within it return to identity at 2\ensuremath{\pi}. The non-compactness of the boost group is the algebraic-shadow articulation of the dynamic expansion of x\ensuremath{_{4}}: rotation into x\ensuremath{_{4}} couples to the x\ensuremath{_{4}}-expansion at velocity c, and since the expansion is open-ended (the x\ensuremath{_{4}}-axis is not bounded above), the rotation-into-x\ensuremath{_{4}} is correspondingly open-ended. The asymptotic boundedness v \ensuremath{\rightarrow} c as \ensuremath{\zeta} \ensuremath{\rightarrow} \ensuremath{\infty} is the algebraic-shadow articulation of the fact that rotation into x\ensuremath{_{4}} cannot exceed the x\ensuremath{_{4}}-expansion velocity c: the universe's expansion rate sets the upper bound on the velocity any spatial-rotation-into-x\ensuremath{_{4}} can achieve.


The three parts together establish that the asymmetry between rotation within (x\ensuremath{_{1}}, x\ensuremath{_{2}}, x\ensuremath{_{3}}) and rotation into x\ensuremath{_{4}} is a direct theorem of dx\ensuremath{_{4}}/dt = ic, with the compact/non-compact distinction and the speed-limit c being the algebraic-shadow articulations of the geometric fact. QED.


### §29.7.3. Ten Empirically-Observed Phenomena Unified by the Asymmetry


The asymmetry of Theorem 29.7.2.1 manifests in at least ten empirically-observed phenomena that the orthodox tradition has documented without recognizing the unified foundational origin. Each phenomenon is, in the McGucken-framework reading, an algebraic-shadow articulation of the fact that rotation within (x\ensuremath{_{1}}, x\ensuremath{_{2}}, x\ensuremath{_{3}}) behaves one way and rotation into x\ensuremath{_{4}} behaves a different way. The present subsection inventories the ten phenomena and identifies their unified origin.


Phenomenon 1 — Boosts vs. rotations have different group-theoretic character. Spatial rotations form the compact group SO(3); boosts form a non-compact subgroup of the Lorentz group. The orthodox tradition documents this as a metric-signature consequence (boosts mix space and time, which have opposite metric signs). The McGucken-framework reading: the compact/non-compact distinction is the algebraic-shadow articulation of the static/dynamic distinction between (x\ensuremath{_{1}}, x\ensuremath{_{2}}, x\ensuremath{_{3}}) and x\ensuremath{_{4}} (Theorem 29.7.2.1).


Phenomenon 2 — The trigonometric/hyperbolic distinction in transformation formulas. Spatial rotations use $\cos\theta$ and $\sin\theta$ (bounded, periodic functions); boosts use $\cosh\zeta$ and $\sinh\zeta$ (unbounded, monotonic functions). The McGucken-framework reading: the trigonometric functions are bounded because the spatial slice is bounded in directional structure (rotation returns to identity at 2\ensuremath{\pi}); the hyperbolic functions are unbounded because the x\ensuremath{_{4}}-axis is unbounded in expansion (rotation into x\ensuremath{_{4}} never closes back on itself).


Phenomenon 3 — The Wigner rotation: a spatial rotation acquires a boost component when applied to a moving frame. When two boosts in different spatial directions are composed, the result is a boost plus an extra spatial rotation (the Wigner angle). The orthodox tradition documents this as the noncommutativity of boosts in the Lorentz group. The McGucken-framework reading: the Wigner rotation is the algebraic-shadow articulation of the fact that "rotation into x\ensuremath{_{4}}" (boost) is not the same operation as "rotation within (x\ensuremath{_{1}}, x\ensuremath{_{2}}, x\ensuremath{_{3}})" — composing two rotations-into-x\ensuremath{_{4}} in different spatial directions produces a residual rotation-within-the-spatial-slice because the x\ensuremath{_{4}}-direction is the same for both boosts but the spatial directions are different.


Phenomenon 4 — Thomas precession: an orbiting spin precesses without any explicit torque. Llewellyn Thomas's 1926 discovery: the spin of an electron orbiting a nucleus precesses at a rate that cannot be accounted for by any torque in the spatial frame. The resolution requires recognizing that the electron's reference frame is continuously boosted as it orbits, and the boost composition produces the Wigner rotation, which precesses the spin. The McGucken-framework reading: Thomas precession is the cleanest empirical signature of the asymmetry — the spin rotates one way under spatial rotation (within the McGucken-Sphere's spatial cross-section) and differently under rotation into x\ensuremath{_{4}} (which couples to the x\ensuremath{_{4}}-expansion direction); the orbital motion involves both kinds of rotation continuously, and the noncommutativity between them produces the precession. The factor-of-½ that Thomas's calculation supplies is the algebraic-shadow articulation of the McGucken-Sphere's SU(2) double-cover of SO(3).


Phenomenon 5 — The anomalous magnetic moment g \ensuremath{\approx} 2 of the electron. The classical magnetic moment of a charged rotating object with angular momentum L is \ensuremath{\mu} = (q/2m)L. For an electron's *spin* angular momentum S, the empirical magnetic moment is \ensuremath{\mu} = g \ensuremath{\cdot} (q/2m) S with g \ensuremath{\approx} 2 — twice the classical value. The orthodox tradition documents this as a relativistic prediction of the Dirac equation. The McGucken-framework reading: the factor-of-2 is the algebraic-shadow articulation of the McGucken-Sphere's SU(2) double-cover of SO(3). A 2\ensuremath{\pi} rotation in SO(3) (the spatial rotation group acting on the McGucken-Sphere) corresponds to a \ensuremath{\pi} rotation in SU(2) (the double-cover acting on the spinor representation), and equivalently the spinor's coupling to the magnetic field acquires the factor-of-2 that the double-cover relationship introduces. The "anomalous" g \ensuremath{\approx} 2 is, not anomalous — it is the expected algebraic-shadow articulation of the McGucken-Sphere's double-cover structure as it interacts with spatial rotation.


Phenomenon 6 — CPT asymmetry, particularly the empirical T-asymmetry of the universe. The CPT theorem of orthodox QFT establishes that the combined operation of charge conjugation C, parity P, and time reversal T is a symmetry of any Lorentz-invariant local QFT. Individually, C, P, and T can be broken; weak interactions break CP (and hence T by CPT). The universe is also empirically T-asymmetric at the cosmological scale: matter dominates over antimatter, the Second Law of Thermodynamics holds with strict monotonicity, and the cosmological arrow of time points unambiguously forward. The McGucken-framework reading: P acts within the spatial slice — it is a discrete operation in the rotation structure on (x\ensuremath{_{1}}, x\ensuremath{_{2}}, x\ensuremath{_{3}}). T acts on the x\ensuremath{_{4}}-axis — it is the discrete operation x_4 \ensuremath{\rightarrow} -x_4, which is the −ic orientation reading of dx\ensuremath{_{4}}/dt = ic. The fact that the universe is not T-symmetric is the empirical signature that the universe has chosen the +ic orientation of the McGucken Principle rather than the −ic orientation. The T-asymmetry is the algebraic-shadow articulation of the universe's foundational +ic orientation, which makes rotation into x\ensuremath{_{4}} asymmetric: there is a forward x\ensuremath{_{4}}-direction (expanding) and a backward x\ensuremath{_{4}}-direction (which the universe does not access).


Phenomenon 7 — The mass-energy equivalence E = mc\ensuremath{^{2}}: particles at rest in the spatial slice still have nonzero energy. Einstein's E = mc\ensuremath{^{2}} supplies the fact that a particle at spatial rest has rest energy E = mc\ensuremath{^{2}}. The orthodox tradition documents this as a consequence of relativistic kinematics. The McGucken-framework reading: a particle at rest in (x\ensuremath{_{1}}, x\ensuremath{_{2}}, x\ensuremath{_{3}}) is *still moving at velocity c in the x\ensuremath{_{4}}-direction*, because x\ensuremath{_{4}} is expanding at c from every event via dx\ensuremath{_{4}}/dt = ic. The energy E = mc\ensuremath{^{2}} is the energy of the particle's motion along x\ensuremath{_{4}} at velocity c. The mass-energy equivalence is the algebraic-shadow articulation of the fact that the four-velocity is the x\ensuremath{_{4}}-velocity is always c. This is the canonical four-fold ontology of the McGucken framework: absolute rest in (x\ensuremath{_{1}}, x\ensuremath{_{2}}, x\ensuremath{_{3}}) = massive particle at spatial rest with full budget into x\ensuremath{_{4}}-motion; absolute rest in x\ensuremath{_{4}} = photon at v=c with full budget into spatial motion.


Phenomenon 8 — The four-velocity constraint u^\ensuremath{\mu} u_\ensuremath{\mu} = -c\ensuremath{^{2}} (or +c\ensuremath{^{2}} depending on signature). The four-velocity u^\ensuremath{\mu} = dx^\ensuremath{\mu}/d\ensuremath{\tau} of any massive particle satisfies u^\ensuremath{\mu} u_\ensuremath{\mu} = -c\ensuremath{^{2}} (in the (-,+,+,+) signature convention). This is the *master equation* of relativistic kinematics, stating that the four-velocity magnitude is always c with the spatial three-velocity v and the x\ensuremath{_{4}}-velocity ẋ_4 exchanging budget along the constraint ẋ_4\ensuremath{^{2}} - |v|\ensuremath{^{2}} = c\ensuremath{^{2}}. The McGucken-framework reading: the four-velocity constraint is the algebraic-shadow articulation of dx\ensuremath{_{4}}/dt = ic as a budget-allocation. The total four-velocity is fixed at c by the McGucken Principle; the spatial velocity and the x\ensuremath{_{4}}-velocity are budget-exchanged as the particle moves. A photon spends its entire budget on spatial motion (v=c, ẋ_4 = 0); a massive particle at rest spends its entire budget on x\ensuremath{_{4}}-motion (v=0, ẋ_4 = c); a moving massive particle splits the budget. The four-velocity constraint is the canonical algebraic articulation of the asymmetry between spatial motion and x\ensuremath{_{4}}-motion, with the total c-speed-budget being the conservation law that ties them together.


Phenomenon 9 — The factor of \ensuremath{i} in time evolution but not in spatial gradients. Both the Schrödinger equation i\ensuremath{\hbar}\ensuremath{\partial}_t\ensuremath{\psi} = H\ensuremath{\psi} and the Dirac equation $i\hbar\partial_t\psi = (\vec{\alpha}\cdot\vec{p}c + \beta mc^2)\psi$ contain an explicit factor of \ensuremath{i} on the time-derivative side, while the spatial gradients $\vec{\nabla}\psi$ have no factor of \ensuremath{i} in front. The orthodox tradition cannot explain this asymmetry — it is part of the "mystery of \ensuremath{i} in QM" that Segal 2021 invokes via the René Thom mystery (§21.6 of the present paper). The McGucken-framework reading: the factor of \ensuremath{i} in i\ensuremath{\hbar}\ensuremath{\partial}_t is the algebraic-shadow articulation of the \ensuremath{i} in dx\ensuremath{_{4}}/dt = ic. The time-derivative \ensuremath{\partial}_t in QM is the operational articulation of the x\ensuremath{_{4}}-derivative via the chain rule \ensuremath{\partial}_t = ic \ensuremath{\partial}_{x\ensuremath{_{4}}}, and the \ensuremath{i} in i\ensuremath{\hbar}\ensuremath{\partial}_t = c\ensuremath{\hbar} \ensuremath{\partial}_x_4 is exactly the perpendicularity-marker of the fourth dimension. The factor of \ensuremath{i} in time evolution but not in spatial gradients is the algebraic-shadow articulation of the asymmetry between x\ensuremath{_{4}} (perpendicular to the spatial slice, marked by \ensuremath{i}) and (x\ensuremath{_{1}}, x\ensuremath{_{2}}, x\ensuremath{_{3}}) (within the spatial slice, with real-valued gradients). The "mystery of \ensuremath{i} in QM" dissolves into the foundational fact of the asymmetry between rotation in the spatial slice and rotation into x\ensuremath{_{4}}.


Phenomenon 10 — Spin precession in magnetic fields with the gyromagnetic ratio's sign and magnitude. A spin in a magnetic field B precesses with frequency \ensuremath{\omega} = (gq/2m)|B|, with the precession occurring *in the spatial plane perpendicular to B*. The precession's direction is determined by the +ic orientation of the Principle — the universe's foundational asymmetry that specifies which way is forward in x\ensuremath{_{4}}. The gyromagnetic precession's direction and magnitude are jointly the algebraic-shadow articulation of the asymmetry, with the magnitude (factor-of-2 from g \ensuremath{\approx} 2) encoding the McGucken-Sphere's double-cover structure and the direction (sign of g) encoding the +ic orientation.


**Theorem 29.7.3.1 (Unification of Ten Phenomena Under the Asymmetry).** *The ten empirically-observed phenomena documented above (Phenomena 1–10) are unified as algebraic-shadow articulations of the asymmetry between rotation within (x\ensuremath{_{1}}, x\ensuremath{_{2}}, x\ensuremath{_{3}}) and rotation into x\ensuremath{_{4}}, with the McGucken Principle dx\ensuremath{_{4}}/dt = ic as the geometric fact from which the asymmetry descends. ### §29.7.4. The Post-McGucken Spinor — Eight Derivations from dx\ensuremath{_{4}}/dt = ic


The McGucken-framework derivation of the spinor establishes the spinor's structure as a chain of theorems from dx\ensuremath{_{4}}/dt = ic. The present subsection supplies the eight derivations, each starting from the foundational principle and arriving at one feature of the spinor's phenomenology.


Derivation 1 — The McGucken-Sphere as the geometric primitive. From dx\ensuremath{_{4}}/dt = ic: every event p \ensuremath{\in} the McGucken Manifold is the apex of a McGucken-Sphere \ensuremath{\mathcal{S}}_p(\ensuremath{\tau}), defined as the spatial 2-sphere of radius c\ensuremath{\tau} centered at p supplied by the x\ensuremath{_{4}}-expansion in time interval \ensuremath{\tau} [46, Theorem 6.1]. The McGucken-Sphere S\ensuremath{^{2}} = \ensuremath{\mathcal{S}}_p(\ensuremath{\tau}) is the canonical geometric object of the McGucken framework, and the spinor's structure emerges as the algebraic-coordinate articulation of representations of the McGucken-Sphere's rotation group.

#### Penrose Articulation 3 — The *Road to Reality* Hartle-Hawking Wick Rotation Passage as Articulation of Five Ingredients of the McGucken Framework


In Chapter 28 of *The Road to Reality* [119, §28.9], Penrose describes the orthodox Wick rotation and the Hartle-Hawking modification with extensive technical detail. The passages, which establish the five ingredients:


The first Penrose ingredient (Euclidean-as-primary) — Euclidean-as-primary. Penrose writes: *"The original (Gian Carlo Wick) idea was that a (special-)relativistic quantum field theory can be constructed by first formulating it with Minkowski spacetime replaced by this Euclidean 4-space \ensuremath{\mathbb{E}}\ensuremath{^{4}}, where the theory is now taken to be invariant under the Euclidean group of symmetries of \ensuremath{\mathbb{E}}\ensuremath{^{4}}. Assuming that the quantities obtained in the Euclidean version of the theory are analytic in the coordinates, the Wick rotation can then be applied, with \ensuremath{\tau} rotated continuously back into \ensuremath{t}, so that we now obtain a corresponding theory that is invariant under the Poincaré group of Minkowski 4-space."* The content: Euclidean signature is treated as the starting point, with Lorentzian signature being recovered through a "rotation back" via the analyticity assumption.


The second Penrose ingredient (compactness asymmetry) — The compactness asymmetry. Penrose writes: *"This procedure has two significant advantages. First, quantities that are liable to be divergent in Minkowski space may turn out to be convergent in the Euclidean version of the theory. (The reason comes down to the Euclidean rotation group O(4) being compact, so of finite volume, whereas the relativistic Lorentz group O(3,1) is non-compact and of infinite volume.) In particular, path integrals have a much better chance of a mathematically meaningful definition in the Euclidean rather than the Minkowskian version."* The content: the Euclidean rotation group O(4) is compact while the Lorentz group O(3,1) is non-compact, with the asymmetry being the reason for the Wick-rotation's calculational advantage.


The third Penrose ingredient (analyticity assumption) — The analyticity assumption and the positive-frequency requirement. Penrose writes: *"The other advantage is that requirements of positive frequency can be ensured by carefully applying the Wick rotation in the correct way."* The content: the positive-frequency requirement (the spectral condition that energies be non-negative) is ensured by the Wick-rotation procedure, with the analyticity assumption being the technical mechanism by which the rotation is performed.


The fourth Penrose ingredient (Hartle-Hawking manifold-level rotation) — The Hartle-Hawking manifold-level rotation. Penrose writes: *"In the Hartle–Hawking scheme, it is necessary to use Hawking's ingenious modification of the Wick idea, in which the 'rotation' is applied not to a space which is a background to the paths, in a path integral — which is the usual idea — but to the individual spacetimes which themselves constitute each path of the path integral. These 'spacetimes' are, accordingly, allowed to have positive-definite Riemannian metrics, rather than the Lorentzian metrics that apply to a normal spacetime."* Penrose then notes Wesley's caveat: *"It should be made clear, however, that there is a 'leap of imagination' involved in the Hawking version of 'Euclideanization' going far beyond that of Wick's original idea. Whether or not this provides a fruitful route to the correct union of general relativity with quantum mechanics remains to be seen."* The content: Hartle-Hawking apply the Wick rotation at the manifold level (to the spacetimes themselves) rather than at the field level (to fields on a fixed background), with Penrose flagging this as a "leap of imagination" of uncertain status.


The fifth Penrose ingredient (no-boundary proposal) — The no-boundary proposal. Penrose writes: *"Hartle and Hawking's striking proposal was that this path-integral approach of Hawking's could describe the relevant quantum theory for the Big Bang itself, and that in place of an actual singular spacetime there would be a quantum superposition (i.e. 'path integral') of 'spacetimes' which could have Riemannian in place of Lorentzian metrics. They referred to their idea as the 'no-boundary' proposal, because rather than having the singular boundary to the classical spacetime..."* The content: the Hartle-Hawking no-boundary proposal applies the manifold-level Wick rotation to cosmological events including the Big Bang, replacing the singular Lorentzian spacetime at t=0 with a non-singular Riemannian-metric quantum superposition.

#### §29.7.9.5.1. The Five-Edition Publication Record and the 32-Year Editorial Constancy of the Channel-A-Only-Reading Commitment


The five-edition publication record of Zinn-Justin's *Quantum Field Theory and Critical Phenomena* is documented from the front-matter copyright page of the Fifth Edition: *"First Edition published in 1989. **Definition 29.7.9.5.1 (Channel-A-Only-Reading Celebration-Without-Foundational-Examination Pattern).** *A canonical-textbook treatment of the Wick rotation exhibits the Channel-A-only-reading celebration-without-examination pattern if and only if it satisfies the following three conditions: (CWE-1) the Wick rotation appears in technical roles across multiple distinct applications (e.g., finite-temperature QFT, instanton methods, Euclidean lattice methods, statistical-mechanics analogies); (CWE-2) the technical applications are developed with mature mathematical rigor across the canonical-textbook register; (CWE-3) no section, subsection, footnote, or appendix at any level of the text examines the physical content of the substitution t \ensuremath{\rightarrow} −i\ensuremath{\tau} — neither identifying it as a physical principle, nor as a coordinate identity, nor as a separator of two channels, nor as a process performed by physical apparatuses, nor as any other physical content. **Remark 29.7.9.5.1.5 (The Pattern's Operational Definition Is Test-Theoretic, Not Sociological).** *Definition 29.7.9.5.1 is test-theoretic, not sociological: the three conditions (CWE-1), (CWE-2), (CWE-3) are conditions on the textual content of the canonical-textbook treatment, verifiable by direct primary-source inspection. The diagnostic is therefore falsifiable in the historical-evidentiary sense: any canonical-textbook treatment that satisfies (CWE-1) and (CWE-2) but fails (CWE-3) — i.e., contains substantive physical examination of the Wick rotation — would refute the diagnostic for that text. The claim of §29.7.9.5 of the present paper is that Zinn-Justin's *Quantum Field Theory and Critical Phenomena* in its five-edition, 32-year, 1074-page canonical record satisfies all three conditions of Definition 29.7.9.5.1, with the satisfaction established by the primary-source evidence of §§29.7.9.5.2–29.7.9.5.3.*

#### §29.7.9.5.8. Historical Synthesis — The Zinn-Justin Canonical-Textbook Record as the Cleanest Specimen of the Channel-A-Only-Reading Celebration-Without-Foundational-Examination Pattern


The historical synthesis of §29.7.9.5 of the present paper consolidates the primary-source evidence of §§29.7.9.5.1–29.7.9.5.6 into the closing diagnostic claim that the Zinn-Justin canonical-textbook record supplies the cleanest specimen of the Channel-A-only-reading celebration-without-examination pattern in the historical-canonical-textbook record.


The cleanness of the specimen is established by four diagnostic factors:

The first diagnostic factor is the scale of the celebration. The 1074-page, 42-chapter, five-edition, 32-year canonical-textbook record supplies the most extensive single-text celebration of the Wick rotation in the historical-canonical-textbook record. The six chapters of instanton methodology (Chapters 37–40, 42), the chapter of finite-temperature methodology (Chapter 33), the ten chapters of critical-phenomena methodology (Chapters 14–19, 31, 32, 36, 41), the Euclidean-default chapter on QM (Chapter 2), and the multiple Wick-theorem celebrations across Chapters 1, 2, and 7 jointly establish a scale of celebration that no other single-text canonical-textbook treatment in the orthodox-tradition record matches.

The second diagnostic factor is the explicitness of the commitment. The five Fifth-Edition-Preface articulations the five Zinn-Justin articulations from the Fifth-Edition Preface of his textbook of §29.7.9.5.2 of the present paper supply explicit canonical-textbook articulations of the Channel-A-only-reading commitment in Zinn-Justin's own words. The explicit matrix realisations of the \ensuremath{\gamma}-matrices in the Dirac basis are \ensuremath{\gamma}\ensuremath{^{0}} = diag(I_2, −I_2) up to scaling, \ensuremath{\gamma}\ensuremath{^{i}} = ((0, \ensuremath{\sigma}\ensuremath{^{i}}), (−\ensuremath{\sigma}\ensuremath{^{i}}, 0)) where \ensuremath{\sigma}\ensuremath{^{i}} are the Pauli matrices, with the multiplications i\ensuremath{\cdot}\ensuremath{\gamma}^\ensuremath{\mu} in the (−, +, +, +) convention yielding (\ensuremath{\gamma}\ensuremath{^{0}})\ensuremath{^{2}} = −I_4, (\ensuremath{\gamma}\ensuremath{^{i}})\ensuremath{^{2}} = +I_4 — verified by SymPy symbolic computation in §29.7.10.6 of the present subsection. \ensuremath{\blacksquare}

#### §29.7.10.6. Step 4 — Operator Square Root (Dirac 1928 Identity; SymPy Symbolic Verification of D\ensuremath{^{2}} = −{\rule{0.7em}{0.7em}} in the (−, +, +, +) Convention)

**Theorem 29.7.10.5 (Dirac Operator Square Identity — Dirac 1928 [3]).** *The Dirac operator D = i\ensuremath{\gamma}^\ensuremath{\mu}\ensuremath{\partial}_\ensuremath{\mu} acting on smooth spinor fields \ensuremath{\psi} \ensuremath{\in} \ensuremath{\Gamma}(S) on the real four-manifold the McGucken Manifold with metric \ensuremath{\eta} of signature (−, +, +, +) satisfies the operator identity D\ensuremath{^{2}} = −{\rule{0.7em}{0.7em}}, where {\rule{0.7em}{0.7em}} = \ensuremath{\eta}^{\ensuremath{\mu}\ensuremath{\nu}}\ensuremath{\partial}_\ensuremath{\mu}\ensuremath{\partial}_\ensuremath{\nu} is the d'Alembertian operator on McGucken Manifold \text{the McGucken Manifold}. **Proof.** Direct computation, with SymPy symbolic verification reproduced below. In components, with \ensuremath{\partial}_\ensuremath{\mu} commuting on smooth functions:

D\ensuremath{^{2}} = (i\ensuremath{\gamma}^\ensuremath{\mu}\ensuremath{\partial}_\ensuremath{\mu})(i\ensuremath{\gamma}^\ensuremath{\nu}\ensuremath{\partial}_\ensuremath{\nu}) = i\ensuremath{^{2}} \ensuremath{\gamma}^\ensuremath{\mu} \ensuremath{\gamma}^\ensuremath{\nu} \ensuremath{\partial}_\ensuremath{\mu} \ensuremath{\partial}_\ensuremath{\nu} = −\ensuremath{\gamma}^\ensuremath{\mu} \ensuremath{\gamma}^\ensuremath{\nu} \ensuremath{\partial}_\ensuremath{\mu} \ensuremath{\partial}_\ensuremath{\nu}.

Since \ensuremath{\partial}_\ensuremath{\mu} \ensuremath{\partial}_\ensuremath{\nu} = \ensuremath{\partial}_\ensuremath{\nu} \ensuremath{\partial}_\ensuremath{\mu} on smooth functions (Schwarz's theorem on the commutativity of partial derivatives), the product \ensuremath{\gamma}^\ensuremath{\mu} \ensuremath{\gamma}^\ensuremath{\nu} \ensuremath{\partial}_\ensuremath{\mu} \ensuremath{\partial}_\ensuremath{\nu} is symmetric in (\ensuremath{\mu}, \ensuremath{\nu}) up to the symmetrisation of the \ensuremath{\gamma}-matrix part:

\ensuremath{\gamma}^\ensuremath{\mu} \ensuremath{\gamma}^\ensuremath{\nu} \ensuremath{\partial}_\ensuremath{\mu} \ensuremath{\partial}_\ensuremath{\nu} = ½(\ensuremath{\gamma}^\ensuremath{\mu} \ensuremath{\gamma}^\ensuremath{\nu} + \ensuremath{\gamma}^\ensuremath{\nu} \ensuremath{\gamma}^\ensuremath{\mu}) \ensuremath{\partial}_\ensuremath{\mu} \ensuremath{\partial}_\ensuremath{\nu} = ½ \ensuremath{\cdot} 2\ensuremath{\eta}^{\ensuremath{\mu}\ensuremath{\nu}} \ensuremath{\cdot} \ensuremath{\partial}_\ensuremath{\mu} \ensuremath{\partial}_\ensuremath{\nu} = \ensuremath{\eta}^{\ensuremath{\mu}\ensuremath{\nu}} \ensuremath{\partial}_\ensuremath{\mu} \ensuremath{\partial}_\ensuremath{\nu} = {\rule{0.7em}{0.7em}}.

Therefore D\ensuremath{^{2}} = −{\rule{0.7em}{0.7em}}. The factorisation of the Dirac equation follows: (i\ensuremath{\gamma}^\ensuremath{\mu}\ensuremath{\partial}_\ensuremath{\mu} + m)(i\ensuremath{\gamma}^\ensuremath{\mu}\ensuremath{\partial}_\ensuremath{\mu} − m)\ensuremath{\psi} = (D + m)(D − m)\ensuremath{\psi} = (D\ensuremath{^{2}} − m\ensuremath{^{2}})\ensuremath{\psi} = (−{\rule{0.7em}{0.7em}} − m\ensuremath{^{2}})\ensuremath{\psi}. Setting this to zero gives ({\rule{0.7em}{0.7em}} + m\ensuremath{^{2}})\ensuremath{\psi} = 0, the Klein-Gordon equation. \ensuremath{\blacksquare}

#### §29.7.10.9. Step 7 — Empirical Confirmation: The Werner 1975 and Rauch-Treimer-Bonse 1975 Neutron-Interferometry Experiments

**Theorem 29.7.10.8 (Empirical Confirmation of the SU(2)-Double-Cover Structure of Fermion Matter — Werner et al. 1975 [331]; Rauch, Treimer, and Bonse 1975 [332]).** *Independent neutron-interferometry experiments by Werner, Colella, Overhauser, and Eagen (Phys. Rev. Lett. 35 (1975) 1053) [331] and by Rauch, Treimer, and Bonse (Phys. Lett. A 54 (1975) 425) [332] empirically demonstrate that the wavefunction of a neutron undergoing a 2\ensuremath{\pi} precession in an external magnetic field acquires a phase shift of \ensuremath{\pi} (i.e., the wavefunction picks up a factor of (−1)), confirming that fermion wavefunctions return to their initial state only after a 4\ensuremath{\pi} precession. The 4\ensuremath{\pi} periodicity is the direct empirical signature of the SU(2)-double-cover structure of fermion matter established in Theorem 29.7.10.7 of the present subsection.*

**Proof of empirical confirmation.** *Part 1 (the Werner 1975 experiment [331]).* Werner and collaborators used a perfect-crystal neutron interferometer at the University of Missouri Research Reactor to split a thermal-neutron beam coherently into two paths, applied a uniform magnetic field B along the direction of propagation in one path, recombined the two paths, and measured the interference pattern as a function of the integral \ensuremath{\int}B\ensuremath{\cdot}dt experienced by the magnetically-influenced beam. The historical content of the spinor-as-square-root-of-dx\ensuremath{_{4}}/dt-=-ic identification spans the 113 years from Cartan's 1913 [333] discovery of the spinor representation to the McGucken 2026 articulation of the physical principle. The arc proceeds in seven significant nodes.

Independent neutron-interferometry experiments empirically confirm the 4\ensuremath{\pi} periodicity of fermion wavefunctions, supplying the empirical anchor for the SU(2) double-cover structure at the matter-physics level. The Atiyah-Singer index theorem, the Dirac operator on a Riemannian manifold, the relationship between spinor bundles and topology — all are unified in a single canonical text. The content is at full mathematical-physics rigour; the physical-principle source of the structure remains unarticulated.

Node 7 — McGucken 2026. The McGucken Principle dx\ensuremath{_{4}}/dt = ic is articulated as the physical-geometric principle from which the Lorentzian metric (Theorem 22.c.6 of §22.c of the present paper, Theorem 29.7.10.2 of the present subsection), the Clifford algebra structure (Theorems 29.7.10.3–29.7.10.4), the Dirac operator and equation (Theorem 29.7.10.5), the exterior-algebra emergence (Theorem 29.7.10.6), the double-cover structure (Theorem 29.7.10.7), and the empirical 4\ensuremath{\pi} periodicity (Theorem 29.7.10.8) jointly descend as derived theorems. The kinematic-sharpening and necessity arguments of §§29.7.10.13–29.7.10.16 establish that, within the class \ensuremath{\mathcal{P}} of perpendicular-imaginary-axis principles dx\ensuremath{_{4}}/dt = \ensuremath{\alpha}i, empirical spinor physics uniquely selects \ensuremath{\alpha} = c. ##### §29.7.10.17.2. The Static-Foursome No-Go Theorem

The principal content of the present subsection is now stated as a theorem.

**Theorem 29.7.10.11 (Static-Foursome No-Go).** *Let C \ensuremath{\in} \ensuremath{\mathcal{Q}}_static be a fully-static-foursome configuration of Definition 29.7.10.2. d\ensuremath{\psi}/d\ensuremath{\tau} = \ensuremath{\sum}_{i=1}^{4} (\ensuremath{\partial}\ensuremath{\psi}/\ensuremath{\partial}x_i) \ensuremath{\cdot} (dx_i/d\ensuremath{\tau}) = \ensuremath{\sum}_{i=1}^{4} (\ensuremath{\partial}\ensuremath{\psi}/\ensuremath{\partial}x_i) \ensuremath{\cdot} 0 = 0.

The empirical observation of fermion-wave-packet propagation in laboratory experiments (cathode-ray-tube electron beams, neutrino fluxes from astrophysical sources, electron-beam interferometry) cannot be reproduced on any C \ensuremath{\in} \ensuremath{\mathcal{Q}}_static. the first limit of the McGucken dx$_4$/dt = ic framework with respect to the Clay Navier–Stokes problem — that the framework does not by itself supply a PDE-level proof of smooth existence or blowup fails on \ensuremath{\mathcal{Q}}_static.

##### §29.7.10.17.4. The Philosophical Implication — Spinors as Empirical Evidence for the Active Reality of Time

The -philosophical content of Theorems 29.7.10.11 and 29.7.10.12 admits the following articulation, which the present subsection states as a separate observation rather than as a formal theorem.

##### §29.7.10.20.1. The Atiyah-Moore Construction — First-Order Dirac Operator Necessity for Exponentiation and the Compton-Cosmological-Constant Two-Parameter Family

Atiyah's verbatim description from the Serre-Festschrift lecture [343, 24:30–28:01]:

> *"We wanted to introduce into physics notions of not just differential operators as usual but also advanced and retarded differential operators... If you have one variable, you take the derivative at a different point — you translate by some amount... Translation has an infinitesimal generator which is differentiation, so translation can formally be written as exponentiating a derivative: if you want to translate by \ensuremath{\alpha}, you exponentiate \ensuremath{\alpha} \ensuremath{\cdot} d/dx. Elementary, just formal restatement of the notion of translation. Now the question is how do you define a relativistically invariant operator when there is no preferred time direction? The whole point of relativity theory is you don't know where time is. So what you need is to use a first-order operator because that's what you need to exponentiate which is relativistically invariant. Well, fortunately Dirac discovered that for us — the Dirac operator was precisely invented by Dirac to find the first-order relativistically-invariant operator and therefore you could use that to define advanced-and-retarded equations. We did that in this little paper and we found by some elementary calculation the possible variables you can use in this equation — there are two variables I call them \ensuremath{\alpha} and \ensuremath{\beta}, two constants... \ensuremath{\alpha} is the amount by which you multiply d/dx — this is related to a physical quantity called the Compton wavelength of the particle so quantum-mechanical notion is involved in deciding on the degree of retardation."*
> — Sir Michael Atiyah, Serre-Festschrift lecture [343, 24:30–28:01]

Atiyah continues at 28:01–29:42:

> *"Then we went on more ambitiously to say: what about Einstein equations, general relativity? Can we write down Einstein equations? And we had some success but only partial. What we did was to use the Dirac operator acting on forms — which is what you need to get general relativity — you take the operator on differential forms d + d* (delta), that's an inhomogeneous operator because one raises degree and one lowers degree, it acts on all the forms like spinors. When you square it, d\ensuremath{^{2}} = 0, \ensuremath{\delta}\ensuremath{^{2}} = 0, you get the Laplace operator which preserves forms — and that's what Hodge did. People emphasize the second-order operator but the first-order operator is more fundamental. If you do that and write down the corresponding story for the spinors then you find that the scalar curvature this time gets replaced by the Ricci curvature, which was known to Bochner, and the Ricci curvature is of course what enters into the Einstein equations. So this at least gives you a bit of a clue as to how the Einstein equations might be... and then you find the other constant in the equation — there were two constants, one was the degree of the shift which we related to the Compton wavelength, the other was the size of the correction term, the retardation parameter which I called \ensuremath{\beta}. Now \ensuremath{\beta} turns out interpreted as a cosmological constant. So the same ideas which lead to quantum mechanics lead in the direction of cosmology."*
> — Sir Michael Atiyah, Serre-Festschrift lecture [343, 28:01–29:42]

The content of the Atiyah-Moore 2010 paper [345], as transcribed from Atiyah's own verbatim primary-source description, is the following catalogue of five findings:

Atiyah's first finding — that the first-order nature of the Dirac operator is essential for exponentiation, contra the orthodox-tradition claim that a second-order operator would suffice *The first-order nature of the Dirac operator is essential for exponentiation*, and the orthodox-tradition "smart Alec" claim that the Dirac operator could be replaced by a second-order operator is incorrect for this purpose. Atiyah's second finding — that exponentiation of the Dirac operator yields a one-parameter family of advanced-retarded operators with parameter $\alpha$ *Exponentiation of the Dirac operator yields a one-parameter family of advanced-retarded operators*, with the parameter \ensuremath{\alpha} specifying the translation amount.

Atiyah's third finding — that the parameter $\alpha$ acquires a physical interpretation as the Compton wavelength of the particle *The parameter \ensuremath{\alpha} acquires a physical interpretation as the Compton wavelength of the particle*, identifying the quantum-mechanical content of the construction.

Atiyah's fourth finding — that extending the construction to act on differential forms via the $(d + d^*)$ operator supplies partial general-relativistic content, with Ricci curvature appearing via Bochner's formula *Extension of the construction to act on differential forms via the (d + d*) operator* (which squares to the Laplace-de-Rham operator on forms) supplies a partial general-relativistic content, with the Ricci curvature appearing (per Bochner's formula).

Atiyah's fifth finding — that the second parameter $\beta$ acquires a physical interpretation as the cosmological constant *The second parameter \ensuremath{\beta} acquires a physical interpretation as the cosmological constant*, identifying the cosmological content of the construction.

The joint conclusion of Atiyah's five findings on the Dirac operator — first-order nature essential for exponentiation, advanced-retarded one-parameter family, $\alpha$ as Compton wavelength, extension to differential forms, and $\beta$ as cosmological constant, in Atiyah's own verbatim summary: "The same ideas which lead to quantum mechanics lead in the direction of cosmology." #### §29.7.10.21. Spinors Without Complex Structure — The Local-Kinematic Source of i\ensuremath{^{2}} = −1 in the McGucken Principle vs. the Global-Topological Source of i\ensuremath{^{2}} = −1 in Complex Manifolds

A important observation Atiyah supplies at timecode 7:24–8:11 of the Serre-Festschrift lecture [343] is the explicit distinction between the *complex-manifold* source of the spinor's algebraic-shadow content (via the Hodge (p, q) decomposition on complex manifolds) and the *intrinsic* spinor structure that exists *without* requiring a global complex structure on the underlying manifold.

##### §29.7.10.21.1. Atiyah's Explicit Distinction — Verbatim Primary-Source Content

Atiyah's verbatim statement [343, 7:24–8:11]:

> *"If the manifold you're studying is complex, then it's well-known to Hodge and so on the differential forms on the manifold can be broken up into the forms of type (p, q), where p involves the dz's and q involves the dz̄'s — the mixture of the two, the tensor product. So when you have a complex structure you see the square root: and the square root is complex geometry. So when you have complex geometry you found a square root inside the real geometry — complex structure has given you a square root. But spinors exist without the need of complex structure. So what is a spinor when there is no complex structure? That's really the question."*
> — Sir Michael Atiyah, Serre-Festschrift lecture [343, 7:24–8:11]

Atiyah's explicit programmatic question — *"What is a spinor when there is no complex structure?"* — identifies the foundational gap in the orthodox tradition's framework. The content of Atiyah's distinction is the following:

*Complex-manifold source of the square-root content.* On a complex manifold M of real dimension 2n, the global complex structure J: TM \ensuremath{\rightarrow} TM satisfying J\ensuremath{^{2}} = −1 induces the (p, q) Hodge decomposition of differential forms, with the holomorphic forms (q = 0) and antiholomorphic forms (p = 0) supplying the "square root" structure relative to the full exterior algebra. This is the global-topological source of the square-root content: the existence of a global integrable complex structure J on the manifold supplies the i\ensuremath{^{2}} = −1 algebraic-shadow content at every tangent space, but the source is a global topological-geometric structure (the existence of J) rather than a local kinematic content.

*Intrinsic spinor structure without complex structure.* Spinors exist on any orientable real Riemannian or pseudo-Riemannian manifold with a spin structure (i.e., with second Stiefel-Whitney class W\ensuremath{_{2}} = 0 per the standard Lawson-Michelsohn 1989 [335, §I.2] content). The spinor structure does *not* require a global complex structure J on the manifold; spinors exist on real four-manifolds (e.g., on the standard Minkowski space, on de Sitter and anti-de Sitter spacetimes, on Schwarzschild and Kerr spacetimes) that do not, in general, admit a global complex structure. Atiyah's question — *what is the source of the i\ensuremath{^{2}} = −1 algebraic-shadow content of the spinor when the manifold has no global complex structure?* — identifies the foundational-source gap.

##### §29.7.10.24.1. Simon Donaldson and His Dimension-4 Mathematical-Uniqueness Discoveries (1982–1986)

Simon Kirwan Donaldson (b. 1957) is the most important of Atiyah's Oxford doctoral students, completing his PhD under Atiyah's supervision in 1983 with the dissertation that established the content of the dimension-4 mathematical-uniqueness thread. Donaldson was awarded the Fields Medal in 1986 (at age 29, for work substantially completed as a graduate student — an exceptional case in the Fields Medal's history) for the discoveries that opened four-dimensional differential topology as a distinct mathematical subfield uniquely tractable through gauge-theoretic methods. The contemporary mathematical-physics positions: Donaldson is currently Permanent Member at the Simons Center for Geometry and Physics, Stony Brook University, and Professor at Imperial College London.

Atiyah's verbatim primary-source description of Donaldson's discoveries at the Serre-Festschrift lecture [343, 21:35–21:54]:

> *"Donaldson, my student, who became very famous when as a graduate student he discovered the remarkable things about dimension four. Fantastic news, something opened up. Four-dimensional geometry suddenly became much richer field, uniquely in dimension four."*
> — Sir Michael Atiyah, Serre-Festschrift lecture [343, 21:41–21:54], identifying his own graduate student Donaldson as the source of the dimension-4 mathematical-uniqueness discoveries

Donaldson's mathematical contributions to dimension-4 differential topology in the 1982–1986 window, catalogued from his canonical primary-source publications [346, 347, 348]:

*the duty of $i$ as the perpendicularity marker of the fourth axis Donaldson's Diagonalisation Theorem (1982) [346].* For a smooth compact simply-connected oriented 4-manifold M with positive-definite intersection form Q on H\ensuremath{^{2}}(M, \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}), the intersection form Q must be diagonalisable over \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} (equivalent to the standard Euclidean inner product \ensuremath{\bigoplus}_k \ensuremath{\langle}1\ensuremath{\rangle} on \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^{b\ensuremath{^{2}}(M)}). The proof uses moduli spaces of anti-self-dual instantons — solutions to the equation F\ensuremath{^{+}} = 0, where F is the curvature 2-form of an SU(2) connection on a principal SU(2)-bundle over M and F\ensuremath{^{+}} denotes the self-dual part under the Hodge ∗-splitting \ensuremath{\Lambda}\ensuremath{^{2}} = \ensuremath{\Lambda}\ensuremath{^{+}} \ensuremath{\oplus} \ensuremath{\Lambda}\ensuremath{^{-}}. The theorem is the first major application of non-linear partial differential equations from gauge theory to differential topology.

*the duty of $i$ as the rotor and phase carrier The Donaldson Invariants (1987) [347].* Using the moduli space of anti-self-dual instantons (or equivalently the moduli space of Yang-Mills minimisers), Donaldson defined new differential-topological invariants of 4-manifolds — polynomial invariants on the second cohomology H\ensuremath{^{2}}(M, \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}) — that distinguish smooth structures on 4-manifolds where the homeomorphism type alone is insufficient. The Donaldson invariants are the canonical contemporary mathematical-physics tool for distinguishing smooth 4-manifolds.

##### §29.7.10.24.2. The Five Facts of Dimension-4 Mathematical Exceptionality

The mathematical uniqueness of dimension 4 catalogued in Donaldson's discoveries the duty of $i$ as the perpendicularity marker of the fourth axis–CPT as the substrate-level SU(2)-double-cover-chirality swap operation per Theorem 29.7.11.3 of §29.7.10.24.1 of the present subsection consolidates into five facts, each of which holds *exclusively in dimension 4* and fails in every other dimension. The five facts are catalogued below with brief derivation; each is identified in §29.7.10.24.5 of the present subsection as algebraic-shadow content of the McGucken-Sphere's 4D-unique spherical-symmetric expansion at velocity c.

*the first factorisation of the real four-dimensional McGucken Manifold per §29.7.10.24.2 Spin(4) \ensuremath{\cong} SU(2)_L \ensuremath{\times} SU(2)_R — the unique product-factorising spin group.* Spin(4) is the *only* spin group Spin(n) (for n \ensuremath{\geq} 3) that factorises as a direct product of two distinct simple Lie groups. The factorisation Spin(4) \ensuremath{\cong} SU(2)_L \ensuremath{\times} SU(2)_R follows from the isomorphism Cl\ensuremath{^{0}}(4) \ensuremath{\otimes} \ensuremath{\mathbb{C}} \ensuremath{\cong} M_2(\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}) \ensuremath{\oplus} M_2(\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}) per [335, §I.4, Table II]. For n = 3: Spin(3) \ensuremath{\cong} SU(2) is simple, no factorisation. For n = 5: Spin(5) \ensuremath{\cong} Sp(2) is simple, no factorisation. For n = 6: Spin(6) \ensuremath{\cong} SU(4) is simple, no factorisation. For n \ensuremath{\geq} 7: Spin(n) is simple. Only n = 4 admits the product-factorisation, with consequence: the spinor representation S = \ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}\ensuremath{^{4}} of Spin(4) decomposes as S = S\ensuremath{^{+}} \ensuremath{\oplus} S\ensuremath{^{-}} with S\ensuremath{^{+}} acted on by SU(2)_L (the left-handed Weyl spinor) and S\ensuremath{^{-}} acted on by SU(2)_R (the right-handed Weyl spinor). This is the chirality decomposition of the Dirac spinor at the 4-dimensional level.

*the second factorisation of the real four-dimensional McGucken Manifold per §29.7.10.24.2 The Hodge ∗-splitting \ensuremath{\Lambda}\ensuremath{^{2}} = \ensuremath{\Lambda}\ensuremath{^{+}} \ensuremath{\oplus} \ensuremath{\Lambda}\ensuremath{^{-}} — unique to dimension 4.* On a real oriented Riemannian n-manifold, the Hodge ∗-operator acts on the bundle of differential k-forms \ensuremath{\Lambda}^k by ∗: \ensuremath{\Lambda}^k \ensuremath{\rightarrow} \ensuremath{\Lambda}^{n−k}, with the consequence that ∗ maps \ensuremath{\Lambda}^k to itself only when n = 2k. The middle-dimensional case 2k = n yields a self-mapping ∗: \ensuremath{\Lambda}^{n/2} \ensuremath{\rightarrow} \ensuremath{\Lambda}^{n/2}, with ∗\ensuremath{^{2}} = (−1)^{k(n−k)} = (−1)^{(n/2)\ensuremath{^{2}}}. For n = 4 (k = 2): ∗\ensuremath{^{2}} = (−1)\ensuremath{^{4}} = +1, yielding a canonical orthogonal splitting \ensuremath{\Lambda}\ensuremath{^{2}} = \ensuremath{\Lambda}\ensuremath{^{+}} \ensuremath{\oplus} \ensuremath{\Lambda}\ensuremath{^{-}} into +1 and −1 eigenspaces of ∗. For other middle-dimensional cases: n = 2 (k = 1) gives ∗\ensuremath{^{2}} = −1 (no eigenspace splitting over \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}); n = 6 (k = 3) gives ∗\ensuremath{^{2}} = −1 (no splitting); n = 8 (k = 4) gives ∗\ensuremath{^{2}} = +1 (splitting), but in n = 8 the structure does *not* couple to spinors in the same way (Spin(8) has triality, but no product factorisation). The \ensuremath{\Lambda}\ensuremath{^{2}} = \ensuremath{\Lambda}\ensuremath{^{+}} \ensuremath{\oplus} \ensuremath{\Lambda}\ensuremath{^{-}} splitting is therefore uniquely consequential in dimension 4, with the (anti-)self-dual decomposition of 2-forms supplying the algebraic content for Donaldson's anti-self-dual instanton equation F\ensuremath{^{+}} = 0.

*the four-dimensional-uniqueness feature — the property that the smooth-structure exotica of Freedman–Donaldson are unique to dimension 4 Yang-Mills conformal invariance — unique to dimension 4.* The classical Yang-Mills action S_{YM} = (1/g\ensuremath{^{2}}) \ensuremath{\int}_M |F|\ensuremath{^{2}}_g dvol_g for a connection A on a principal G-bundle over M (with F = dA + A \ensuremath{\wedge} A the curvature 2-form) is conformally invariant under metric rescalings g \ensuremath{\rightarrow} \ensuremath{\Omega}\ensuremath{^{2}}g if and only if dim(M) = 4. The proof: |F|\ensuremath{^{2}}_g = g^{\ensuremath{\mu}\ensuremath{\alpha}} g^{\ensuremath{\nu}\ensuremath{\beta}} F_{\ensuremath{\mu}\ensuremath{\nu}} F_{\ensuremath{\alpha}\ensuremath{\beta}} scales as \ensuremath{\Omega}\ensuremath{^{-}}\ensuremath{^{4}} under g \ensuremath{\rightarrow} \ensuremath{\Omega}\ensuremath{^{2}}g, while dvol_g scales as \ensuremath{\Omega}^n where n = dim(M); the integrand scales as \ensuremath{\Omega}^{n−4}, which is conformally invariant iff n = 4. This is the unique dimension in which Yang-Mills theory has classical conformal symmetry, with the consequence that the moduli space of Yang-Mills instantons enjoys conformal-equivariance properties unavailable in other dimensions.

*the resolution of why the $(1,3)$ signature describes reality rather than the $(2,2)$ split signature — the $+ic$ monotonicity of dx$_4$/dt = ic forces $(1,3)$ per Theorem 21.7.14ter.2 Middle-dimensional self-intersection on H\ensuremath{^{2}}(M, \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}) — first non-trivial in dimension 4.* For a smooth compact oriented n-manifold M, the cup product H^k(M, \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}) \ensuremath{\times} H^{n−k}(M, \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}) \ensuremath{\rightarrow} H^n(M, \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}) \ensuremath{\cong} \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} supplies a non-degenerate pairing by Poincaré duality. The middle-dimensional case 2k = n gives a self-pairing H^{n/2}(M, \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}) \ensuremath{\times} H^{n/2}(M, \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}) \ensuremath{\rightarrow} \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}. For n = 2 (k = 1): the self-pairing on H\ensuremath{^{1}} is anti-symmetric, gives a symplectic form (trivial in the simply-connected case). For n = 4 (k = 2): the self-pairing on H\ensuremath{^{2}} is *symmetric* and quadratic, gives the canonical *intersection form* Q: H\ensuremath{^{2}}(M, \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}) \ensuremath{\rightarrow} \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} which is the central topological invariant of the 4-manifold. For n = 6 (k = 3): the self-pairing on H\ensuremath{^{3}} is anti-symmetric (symplectic). For n = 8 (k = 4): the self-pairing on H\ensuremath{^{4}} is again symmetric, but the higher-dimensional setting is mathematically less tractable. Dimension 4 is the *smallest* dimension where the middle-dimensional intersection form is symmetric-quadratic, and is the dimension where this structure is most directly tractable via gauge-theoretic methods.

*the question of why the Fargues-Fontaine curve at every finite prime and the twistor $\mathbb{P}^1$ at the archimedean prime share the same mathematical structure — articulated by Conjecture 21.7.14ter.1 Exotic \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}\ensuremath{^{4}} — uncountably many smooth structures, unique to dimension 4.* For n \ensuremath{\in} {1, 2, 3}: every smooth structure on \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}\ensuremath{^{n}} is diffeomorphic to the standard one (classical result, Moise 1952 for n = 3 and earlier for n = 1, 2). For n \ensuremath{\in} {5, 6, 7,...}: every smooth structure on \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}\ensuremath{^{n}} is diffeomorphic to the standard one (Stallings 1962, Zeeman 1962). For n = 4: there exist *uncountably many* distinct smooth structures on \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}\ensuremath{^{4}}, none diffeomorphic to the standard one (Donaldson-Freedman 1982–1983 [346, 349]). This is the most striking dimension-4 uniqueness fact: \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}\ensuremath{^{4}} is the only Euclidean space that admits multiple smooth structures, and it admits uncountably many.

The five facts the five factorisations of the real four-dimensional McGucken Manifold articulated across §29.7.10.24.2 are *all* dimension-4-specific. Each fails in every other dimension. The foundational question Donaldson's work raised — *why is dimension 4 mathematically exceptional in these five distinct ways?* — is not answered by the orthodox-tradition framework, which catalogues the facts without identifying their physical-geometric source. The McGucken-framework reading developed in §§29.7.10.24.3–29.7.10.24.6 of the present subsection supplies the foundational source.

##### §29.7.10.24.3. The McGucken-Sphere — The Geometric Object Generated Uniquely in 4D by dx\ensuremath{_{4}}/dt = ic

The McGucken-Sphere is the geometric object of the McGucken framework, generated by the principle dx\ensuremath{_{4}}/dt = ic operating at every event of the real four-manifold the McGucken Manifold. The construction is canonical and is developed in detail in corpus paper [42] (Father Symmetry) and the present paper's §22.c (Theorem 22.c.5). The content is summarised below for the present subsection's purposes.

**Definition 29.7.10.4 (The McGucken-Sphere).** *At every event e \ensuremath{\in} the McGucken Manifold, the McGucken-Sphere is the spherically-symmetric wavefront generated by dx\ensuremath{_{4}}/dt = ic operating from e, parametrised by the worldline parameter \ensuremath{\tau} \ensuremath{\in} \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}\ensuremath{_{+}} as:*

*\ensuremath{\mathcal{S}}_e(\ensuremath{\tau}) = {p \ensuremath{\in} the McGucken Manifold: ds(e, p) = ic \ensuremath{\cdot} \ensuremath{\tau} along worldlines from e},*

*where ds is the McGucken-induced Lorentzian line element ds\ensuremath{^{2}} = (dx\ensuremath{_{1}})\ensuremath{^{2}} + (dx\ensuremath{_{2}})\ensuremath{^{2}} + (dx\ensuremath{_{3}})\ensuremath{^{2}} − c\ensuremath{^{2}}(dt)\ensuremath{^{2}} of Theorem 22.c.6 of §22.c. The McGucken-Sphere at parameter \ensuremath{\tau} is a 3-sphere S\ensuremath{^{3}}_\ensuremath{\tau} in the (x\ensuremath{_{1}}, x\ensuremath{_{2}}, x\ensuremath{_{3}}, x\ensuremath{_{4}}) configuration: the boundary of a 4-ball B\ensuremath{^{4}}_\ensuremath{\tau} of "radius" ic \ensuremath{\cdot} \ensuremath{\tau} in the McGucken-Sphere expansion.*

The McGucken-Sphere has the following five -foundational properties.

**Property 29.7.10.1 (The McGucken-Sphere is a 4D Object).** *The McGucken-Sphere exists in (1 active + 3 static)-dimensional configuration. The boundary of the McGucken-Sphere at parameter \ensuremath{\tau} is the 3-sphere S\ensuremath{^{3}}_\ensuremath{\tau} in (x\ensuremath{_{1}}, x\ensuremath{_{2}}, x\ensuremath{_{3}})-space, and the interior is the 4-ball B\ensuremath{^{4}}_\ensuremath{\tau} in (x\ensuremath{_{1}}, x\ensuremath{_{2}}, x\ensuremath{_{3}}, x\ensuremath{_{4}})-configuration. The McGucken-Sphere is intrinsically a 4-dimensional structure: it has 1 "radial" dimension (x\ensuremath{_{4}}, the active expansion direction) and 3 "angular" dimensions (the S\ensuremath{^{3}} boundary). No analogous construction exists in any other dimension: in 3D you would have a (1 + 2) configuration with S\ensuremath{^{2}} boundary (not the McGucken-Sphere); in 5D you would have a (1 + 4) configuration with S\ensuremath{^{4}} boundary (and S\ensuremath{^{4}} has no Lie group structure, breaking the spinor framework). The McGucken-Sphere is mathematically a 4D-unique object.*

**Property 29.7.10.2 (The S\ensuremath{^{3}} Boundary is the Unique Sphere That Is a Lie Group of Dimension \ensuremath{\geq} 1).** *The 3-sphere S\ensuremath{^{3}} admits the structure of a Lie group, with S\ensuremath{^{3}} \ensuremath{\cong} SU(2) \ensuremath{\cong} Sp(1) \ensuremath{\cong} Unit Quaternions. The classical classification of spheres with Lie group structure (Adams 1960, in the famous "Hopf invariant one" theorem [352]): the only spheres that admit Lie group structure are S\ensuremath{^{0}} \ensuremath{\cong} \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/2\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}, S\ensuremath{^{1}} \ensuremath{\cong} U(1), and S\ensuremath{^{3}} \ensuremath{\cong} SU(2). S\ensuremath{^{7}} admits the structure of a Moufang loop (the unit octonions) but not a Lie group. All other spheres S\ensuremath{^{n}} (n \ensuremath{\in} {2, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9,...}) admit no group structure of any kind. Among spheres of dimension \ensuremath{\geq} 1, only S\ensuremath{^{1}} and S\ensuremath{^{3}} are Lie groups; among these, S\ensuremath{^{3}} \ensuremath{\cong} SU(2) is the unique 3-sphere that bounds a McGucken-Sphere in the (1 + 3)-dimensional active-static configuration of Theorem 29.7.10.12 of the present subsection.*

**Property 29.7.10.3 (The Spherical Symmetry Group of S\ensuremath{^{3}} is SO(4), with Double Cover Spin(4) \ensuremath{\cong} SU(2)_L \ensuremath{\times} SU(2)_R — the Unique Product-Factorising Spin Group).** *The rotational symmetry group of the 3-sphere boundary S\ensuremath{^{3}} of the McGucken-Sphere is SO(4), with double cover Spin(4) \ensuremath{\cong} SU(2)_L \ensuremath{\times} SU(2)_R — the unique spin group Spin(n) (n \ensuremath{\geq} 3) that factorises as a direct product of two simple Lie groups, per the first factorisation of the real four-dimensional McGucken Manifold per §29.7.10.24.2 of §29.7.10.24.2 of the present subsection. The two SU(2) factors correspond to the left-action and right-action of unit quaternions on the unit-quaternion-3-sphere: SU(2)_L acts as (q \ensuremath{\mapsto} pq) for p \ensuremath{\in} SU(2), SU(2)_R acts as (q \ensuremath{\mapsto} qp̄) for p \ensuremath{\in} SU(2). Under the McGucken-framework identification of Theorem 29.7.10.7 of §29.7.10.8 of the present subsection, SU(2)_L is the matter-orientation factor (+ic) and SU(2)_R is the antimatter-orientation factor (−ic).*

**Property 29.7.10.4 (The McGucken-Sphere Expansion is Conformally Invariant).** *The McGucken-Sphere expansion at velocity +ic from every event is conformally invariant: the conformal-rescaling g \ensuremath{\rightarrow} \ensuremath{\Omega}\ensuremath{^{2}}g preserves the spherical-symmetric expansion structure at velocity c (the velocity c is itself a derived constant of the principle, not affected by metric rescaling at the kinematic level). The conformal-invariance of the McGucken-Sphere expansion is the physical-geometric source of the conformal-invariance of Yang-Mills theory in dimension 4 (per the four-dimensional-uniqueness feature — the property that the smooth-structure exotica of Freedman–Donaldson are unique to dimension 4 of §29.7.10.24.2) — both express the same underlying conformal symmetry of the active expansion at velocity c.*

**Property 29.7.10.5 (The McGucken-Sphere Generates the Hopf Fibration S\ensuremath{^{3}} \ensuremath{\rightarrow} S\ensuremath{^{2}}).** *The 3-sphere boundary S\ensuremath{^{3}} of the McGucken-Sphere admits the canonical Hopf fibration S\ensuremath{^{1}} \ensuremath{\rightarrow} S\ensuremath{^{3}} \ensuremath{\rightarrow} S\ensuremath{^{2}}, where the S\ensuremath{^{2}} base is the projective space \ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}\ensuremath{^{1}} \ensuremath{\cong} S\ensuremath{^{2}} and the S\ensuremath{^{1}} fibre encodes the U(1) phase. The Hopf fibration is unique among sphere fibrations in low dimensions: it is the foundational example of a non-trivial principal U(1) bundle. Under the McGucken-framework reading, the Hopf fibration is the algebraic-shadow content of the U(1) gauge symmetry of electromagnetism emerging from the McGucken-Sphere's S\ensuremath{^{3}}-boundary structure, per corpus paper [1, §IV] (the electroweak gauge group derivation).*

The five properties (29.7.10.1)–(29.7.10.5) jointly establish the McGucken-Sphere as the geometric object of the McGucken framework, with mathematical structure unique to dimension 4. The next subsection establishes the formal theorem connecting the McGucken-Sphere's 4D-uniqueness to Donaldson's discoveries.
